LIFE IN PATAGONIA
AN EARLESTOWN MAN'S EXPERIENCES.
In the Earlestown Good Templar lodge room, on Monday night, Mr. J. Roberts, a former member

and who for the past six years has been resident in Patagonia, gave an address upon his experiences and treatment whilst there. The ad- dress was of an interesting character, and of the utmost importance to those who may have thoughts of visiting that far off country. Mr. Roberts is an old Earlestown resident, and is by trade a ship

carpenter. In the year 188. he formed one of a party of 470 persons who left England for the Chubut valley in Patagonia, Sonth America, having been promised employment on a new railway being constructed there, and a grant of land. The rail- way was to be 48 miles long, and to stretch across a desert from the seaport into the settlement of Chubut. Mr. Roberts explained that he was fortun- ate in making an agreement with the Railway Co.. to serve them as a leading hand in the construction of the line. After working in the capacity for about 11 months, lie disagreed with the engineer,and left the service. Ile then went down into the valley and started business on his own account, on a small scale,but three months afterwards he bad the mis- fortune to have his place destroyed by fire,en tailing a loss of about £3OO. He was then practically des- titute, but he struggled on, and in time managed to get together a fair business. Speaking of the fate of the others who accompanied him from Enszland, lie said before they started they made agreement to receive a certain amount ner week as wages, but. when they arrived on the spot, the manager of the company called all the men together and induced them to accent their wages in paper money. The paper meney out there rose and fell according to the money market; it had been 5 dollars in tile X, and as much as 23 dollars in the X. The men were persuaded to accept this arrangement, and the manager was thus enabled to put into his own pocket out of their wages, every week,a respectable sum. By this and other questionable systems, the manager was able to build himself a large house, without drawing on his own resources to any great extent. There was no food for the 400 the second day after they arrived, nor could they get it, if there had been, being without funde. The ' company paid their passage out, and they had tci refund in course of time to the company, but they never heard any more of the grant of land. Then , they became short of water, and the sufferings I of the poor people were frightful. Ile saw scores of men come down to the place where he was, with their lips cracked and their tongues swollen, for want of water. During thel whole of the time the line was in course ] of construction the men had practically to fight the company for a little to eat and drink, and if ' they murmured, the managers would say they bad better say nothing, or he would soon have some Italians in their places. Still the suffering for , want of water was very great. It very seldom rained, and during the last four years there had been but one shower of rain which lasted 10 minutes ; the ground was as dry in a few minutes afterwards, as if it had never rained. The men at ' the camp had often to drink salt water. It was true bullock wagons came from the settlement with water, but they could not get all over the camp. The men had a meeting with the chief engineer, and asked him if he could not find them some- thing different to salt water, but the only satisfac- tion they could get was that the company were not forced to find water They not only suffered from want of water, but they did not receive th3ir wages its full, as by the arrangement they made with regard to the paper money, the manager was able to put a portion of their wages into his and the company's pockets. Mr. Roberts's agreement ' was for wages according to English value. but still they tried it on, dropping it about Si. per week. This he allowed to run on for about eight months, but he ultimately demanded the balance of his wages and 100 per cent. in addition, and strange to say he got what he asked for, after some plain speak- ing. Several of the 400 men were still out there, but many had returned to England, while others were (wing fairly well in Buenos Ayres, Many would like to return home, but they had not the means, and it was quite likely they would have to stay there until they got assistant*. The sufferings of tile menoviio had been lured ovar 7,000 miles under false promises, could not be imagined. It was a place he could not recommend anyone to go out to ; in fact be would not like to send a dog there. (Laughter.) On the motion of Bro. Taylor seconded by Bro. Clarke, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Roberts for bis address.

div.head: CHURCHES STRUCK BY LIGHTNING.
div.p: CHURCHES STRUCK BY LIGHTNING.

15 PERSONS KILLED. Not less than three cases of churches being struck by lightning, and in two instances with disastrous results, occurred on Sunday in the Spanish provinces. The worst fatality was as a place called Mekas, in the pro- vince of Orense. Being Sunday, the parish church was crowded with worshippers hearing Mass, when , the lightning struck the sacred edifice, and ten persons r were killed on the spot, while 28 were injured. At about the same time another church at Mucientes, in Valladolid, experienced a similar visitation. Here also a large congregation was gathered inside the building, and equally fatal results ensued, five people being killed and several injured. The famous cathedral at Burgos was likewise struck by lightning on Monday, the force of the electric current displacing a large stone. This cathedral is still unprovided with a lightning conduc- tor. WARRINGTON BOARD OF :GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning. Mr. R. Heaton presided, and there were also present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Balharry, Davies, Hood-W right, Dobson, Ratcliffe, Pilling, Hibbert, A. Jolley, OHL Longton, A. J. Jolley, Hill, Shaw, Smith, Fairclough, Dignum, Aukland, Clarke, W. Houghton, Swinton, Mather ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and other officials. INCREASE IN THE NUMBER OF LUNATICS. The CLERIC remarked upon the increase in the num- ber of lunatics in the Union. The number at present chargeable to the Union was 141.—Mr. W. HOUGHTON asked if any reason could be given for this increase. Had the Ship Canal anything to do with it ?—The CLERIC said a number of cases had been traced to the Ship Canal. The Ship Canal had contribut3d to ' the increase more than any one other cause.— Mr. RATCLIFFE and Mr. LONOTON thought inquiry ought to be made from the Asylum Boards as , to the cause of the increased charges for the mainten- ance of lunatics.—The Chairman said they had really no power o•tor these charges, I the reply to any in- quiry would probably be that only necessary expendi- ture was incurred. In the course of some further conversation, the Clerk said he had been informed that extra expense had been incurred at Rainhill asylum owing to the dangerous character of some of the lunatics sent there, as compared with lunatics in other asylums who came from rural districts.— Mr. Hood-Wright remarked that the dignity of some ot the inmates of the asylums was highly offended by their" being associated with criminal lunatics.—The CLSRIK said the dignity of some of the lady lunatics was beyond comprehension. (Laughter.) FADOATE SCHOOLS. The Padgate Schools Committee recommended that the children have the usual holiday on Walking Day, and railway fares paid to Warrington. Mr. and Mrs. Vaughan, of Saltley, were appointed tailor and foster mother of no. 1 home of the schools.—The minutes were passed.

"HOW SHALL WE DECIDE THIS QUESTION ?" Now, which is the worse—to have no appetite for your dinner, or to have no dinner for your appetite? There are lots of people on the one side or the other of this question. When " good digestion waits on appetite and health on both," that is the ideal attitude of a person towards his meals. But most of us are not blessed in that way, we either have too much food without an appetite, or a vigorous appetite without enough to satisfy it. Different folk will answer this question differently, yet the common sense of it i 3 that, within reasonable limits, it is better to have an appetite without a dinner, because, short of the starvation line, a hungry man is a healthy man ; whereas a man who ought to eat and doesn't feel like eating, stands in need of " alterations and repairs." To illustrate. We recently received a communication in which the writer says, " "I was afraid to eat." Did he fancy his food was poisoned, or did his nature rebel against the nourishment lived on? If the latter, why ? Let him clear the mystery himself. He says, "In the year 1889 I changed my work from railway porter to signalman. I had been signalman twelve months, and then all at once, so to speak, I did not feel myself. My mouth tasted bad, so that ordin- ary articles of diet seem ed to lose their flavour ; the palate, to put it in that way, appeared to have nothing to say to them. One thing was like another, and none was good. My tongue was coated and furred, with a dark line down the middle and yellow fur round it. My 1 breath va sva the poor, wi ,ure, ' were

through the chest and shoulders, which ways right before I had eaten anything. Then I was greatly troubled with wind. It would uather so it felt like a ball in my throat, and act as if it would choke me." We cannot wonder that under these circumstances our friend failed to do justice to his meals. He adds that there was what he calls " a pricking sensation" at his heart, as though it were touched with some sharp in- strument. Then, again, at times he was attacked with spasms, the agony of which was so severe that the sweat rolled off him. "I dreaded," he says," the thought of eating, and many a scanty meal have I made, for I was afraid to eat. "After a time I got into a low, weak, nervous condi- tion, and felt miserable, as if something was going to happen, and this caused me to lose a good deal ef sleep." What he means by the fear of "something going to happen" is, of course, the fear of some calamity, such as the loss of his position, his own death, or the death of somebody dear to him. This was due, as he intimates, to the impoverished state of his blood (the life bearer), his unstrung nerves, and to the brain enfeebled by lack of nourishment. The night of this form of illness is always fall of ghosts and goblins, the creatures of a rest- less and ungoverned imagination. "With great difficulty," he says, "I stuck to my work, for I had a wife and family dep ending on me. So I struggled on, but what I suffered for over two years is put my powers of dese.ription. I am sure no one has suffered so much as I have done." In the latter statement he is undoubtedly wrong. One's own pain is one's own, andis always harder to hear than is one's notion of his neighbour's pain. There is a countless multitude who are all the while going through the same wretched experience, only we don't happen to come in touch with them. Well, the writer finally mentions that after all medi- cal treatment had left him where it found him he chanced to read in a book of a case exactly like his own having been cured by Mother Seigel's Syrup. "My wife," he says, "got me a bottle at Mr. Langstaff's, in Woodlesford, and after using its contents the ailment left me and has never returned since that fortunate day. I should like the whole world to know what it did for me. I have been employed by the Midland Railway Company for eleven years. (Signed) "GEORGE Hula, "Car Bottom-road, " Apperley Bridge, near Leeds. We publish this by Mr. Hunt's desire, in order that part of the world at least may know how thankful he is and for what reason.

div.p: THE VTULLEY FRAUDS.
ANOTHER SUICIDE.

On Monday evening Mr. William Holt, an old man who lived at Strawberry Bank, Blackburn, was. found dead in the cellar of his house with a razor in his hand and a fatal wound in his throat. He had been much de- pressed since the crash caused by the frauds of the late Henry Stanley 'Whalley, the solicitor whb is responsible for widespread distress in Lancashire and Yorkshire. He was trustee for an estate that had been left in Whalley's hands.

THE PRINCE OF BULGARIA'S VISIT PO ENGLAND. RUMOURS Or A MATRIMONIAL ALLIANCE. The excellent reception given to the Prince of Bul- garia in England strengthens (says the Berlin corres- pondent of the " Standard ") the opinion prevalent here that be will betroth himself to an English princess. In some circles here it is asserted that the prince aspires to the hand of one of the Prince of Wales's daughters. Nothing is of course kn3wn for certain on this point, but confirmation of the report is awaited with much interest.

it. But sh-ii cola not manage to finish her soutanes as she meant to do. There were not many lies that stuck in her throat, but this one of loving like brother and sister did. She had never loved him, save in one wild, passionate way, and she never would. Sir Lancelot would have been more than a man, had he not wavered a little in his conviction of her

guilt. He was too unobservant and too deeply engrossed with his own wrongs to interpret her emotion in its trim significance. It appeared to him as the sorrow of one falsely accused, and accused by an almost brother. Besides, after all; what motive had she for Acting as he fancied she had? It was very 'difficult to find one. Was it possible that Jack was in the wrong,. and had simply imagined all the horrors 'he had spoken during the hours of his delirium? Or were they merely the sad conso., quenees of that delirium? ' Andyet, the hints, the subtle poison which, she had instilled into his own ears?, How account for this, save from the workiugs of malice? His face grew dark again, and his cousinls pathos ceased toaffAct him. "You are false, Dorothy Breamish, false as belt! You have deluded me, and led me on to my own misery; led me on to murder--pretty nigh! But it is too late, now to practise your devilish arts upon me. Nothing you could say or do would ever in- duce me to believe in you again. Woman, when' think upon the agony you have made me suffer, I hate you with a savage hatred ' • but when Ithink upon what you may have caused to her—my sweet, soft, beautiful Silvia—then I could kill you with my own. hands. Are you not afraid of rayjust retributhm, you cruel woman?" The fury of his wrongs was on Sir Lancelot; se , ho paced restlessly up and down, and every now Andagain stopped toglare at Madam. But Dorothy Breamish was too true a Callerley to be cowed by his anger. It excited her; but her spirit rose at once to meet it, as though it were a challenge. She admired him more than ever while possessed by the wild passion which was so near akin to her own.. The danger of his wrath intoxicated her like wine. Let him kill her! Death itself, coming, from his hands would be a sort of ecstasy. Their eyes met and flashed together like two swords leaping from their scabbards, and crossing in glorious warfare. , '.l.len she threw herself upon her knees, and hel her clasped hapds pp to hilt'. "No, I am not afraid 1". she said, her voice ring- ing out like a silver trumpet, "I could never be afraid of you, Lancelot 1 Kill meif it pleases you, and I will make no resistance ; see here is my bosom , bared for your blow. I would ,rather have death from you, than life from another." Sir Lancelot looked at her in amazement. Gone in an instant was the smooth, soft-spoken, plausible woman of the world, and before him knelt instead a creature breathing fire and flame, a creature sublime in great and consuming passion. What strange mystery was this revealing itself to his dulled senses? "You have conquered me," she went on in the same clear tone, "I will tell you no more lies now —never, never! Everything you have accused me of is true and—,and more My sins are as scarlet, and I confess them all 1 Only—only, do not hate me, Lancelot. Kill me first, ,dear, and then be a little sorry for me ; but do no quite hate me ! " The clear music of her voice died down to a moan, and thrilled through the air, like the sad wind creeping over the tops of pine trees. "What do you mean? And hew dare you con- fess your shamelessness to me? Rise, Dorothy Breamish, and explain the reason of your conduct. Kneel to the one you have wronged the most, and ask her forgiveness • kneel, if you think meet, to the God whom you Lave outraged by your lies ;but I will not have you kneel to me." Dorothy Breamish rose at his command. Her face was white to the lips. "Do you mean your wife? Think you I would humble myself at her feet? It is to you, and to you only, I pray for mercy ; and if the mercy comes in the guise of death, why, so much the better. I deserve my fate, but I will only accept it from your hands." "Why do you hate hate SiDria ?" " Why ? ! you are a man, or you would not need to ask that question. A woman would have guessed long ago. I. hate her because hove

you."— " Yon love me? Love, me? Why ?" "How do I know? Because you are of the flame temper end of the same blood, perhaps? Was not -brought up to love. you? What name elid I hear in my childhood„ but only that of Lancelot, Lancelot? You know the sort of life we led, shut up and secluded fromlthe. world, your mother and I; and how neither her health nor inclination allowed her to keep up. any intercourse with the people living near. Everything was against my caring for any other man. One needs must love what one knows best, if it is lovable; and a.woman cannot live without a passion." "Do you call that sort of thing love?" asked the baronet, with scorn "you make the same mistake I once made,, and v:sell supreme selfishness by the sacred name of levee." "You are hard aawi.nnjust," murmured Mrs. Breamiah, remvachfully. "Do not expect any gentle dealing's from me ! You say truly when you say we are &hire in many respects.. But de not fancy that therefore I shall be lenient to your-faults. I hate and loathe in you the same things which I hate and loathe in myself. In one thing, however, we are different, thank God. At least lam not treacherous. Where I hate, I 'do not make pretence of love, and fawn upon the. creature whose destruction lam compassing. As, for your so-called love, you ought to be ashamed even to speak of it, Dorothy Breamish.; you, a wife, and a mother l Why did you marry with a lie in. your heart, since you could never care for the man. you promised to love, honour, and obey? Poor, hmmst„ ill-treated Harry Breamish might have been. happy enough, had you been merciful, and left him alone. "I am not the first who married without love, ?ler will Ihe the last ! You, yourself Lancelot, Imwever much your infatuation for a baby face. may have grown upon you since—you were not specially in love with you wife at the time of marriage. Did you not once confess as much to, me? And as for poor Harry—do not think for a, moment that I am not sorry for him aleo. A milkmaid would have pleased him more and made him twenty times happier than I could ever have done." The contemptuous pity of her tone would prob- ably not have gratified the Squire. "You forget your boy when you talk like that," went on the baronet, sternly. "My boy, who is so like you—who ought to have had another father I He could not fail to be a true Callerley, since the man I loved was never out of my thoughts before I gave him birth." "I will not stay longer near you to hear you degrade your womanhood, My blood is cooler now, and reason tells me to leave you alone, as utterly unworthy of my resentment. But know that, if possible. I hate and despise you more than ever, since you told me your wretched secret. Never uncle, • circumstances could I have loved you—you W _cern to me an embodiment of my own evil self And now let me, in leaving, assure you of this ! Your devilish malice has failed-- failed completely. Silvia and I are one in heart, and soul, and body now, and nothing can ever part us, save death; and even death may only mean un- ending love, eternal happiness." Another moment and Dorothy Breamiah was lone. Alone with her misery and her despair. A storm of agony raged over and whirled her fn spirit upon its mighty blast, like one of the dying leaves from the trees. "Autumn is all round me, winter is near," she said, in her wild, excited mood, "near to my heart, as to the heart of nature I But a winter ought by rights to be preceded by a summer, and where, oh God of nature, has my summer been? Every failing leaf is to me a record of hopes that have died within me, stillborn the air is full of farewell to dreams which I have known to be merely dreams, even while I dreamt them. I did not create myself and give myself this hungry soul. Had I made it and been resperup?le for its wants, I would certainly have satisfied It seems to me that God is kinder to His wild creatures than to the human being whom He has created with ungovernable passions like to diem. Had any heart been satisfied, then I should not have winter came, even though tcahraetdwilizr Am I going mad, I wonder? B•sre rue theit "Let winter come since he hates me for the evil I have wrought. Darkness, disaster, and despair, I will welcome all of you now, in the greater storm of my_ misery." ROW long is this =restful calm to continue? I long for the wind to rise, Mid the sea to sob and moan, and the rain to beat down pitilessly, and the sound of death and desolation to peal out and drown my tortured, lonely cry. Why should I alone be wretched, I alone be in pain? Is this =divas:

div.head: CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
div.p: THE CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "Wftere the ..Yorth Wind Blows," dtc.,
dIIAPTER L.

MADAM IN A STORMY MOOD. The autumnal sun was drooping low in the heavens, and its level rays were striking upon the trunks of the few dwarfish trees which grew alongside the lady's walk at Breamish Hall, as Madam paced there, sad and solitary. When this effect struck her, and she noted how it dyed them crimson, end how everything around the small pond at the end of the walk—the dying fronds of the ferns that drooped on the water, the leaves 'that floated upon its surface—how they all partook of the same sanguinary hue, a shudder passed through her frame, and quickly she turned her back upon the reflection and faced the light. "Everywhere blood_ All of the same colour, look where I may," she muttered in a strange, hoarse sort of whisper, "Is it a haunting memory or a prophesy, I wonder? My hand against every- one, and everyone's hand against inn! Nlthat matter? I am amongst the might-havarbeens of life, and there is no help for it now." Whenever Madam was in one of her wild moods, or, as the Squire phrased it, in one of her " tantSums," she sought refuge in this dark, shaded walk, and no one dared there to disturb her privacy. It was a gloomy place, and was probably invested by popular superstition with a ghost, like other walks of like nature; which kept it still more sacred to the mistress of the hall. If there was a change for the worse in the ap- pearance of Squire Breamish, there was certainly one still more marked in that of his wife. Her cheeks had grown thin and hollow, and her eyes— always the unquiet feature in her fine face— glittered and moved restlessly about like those of a beast of prey. Yet withal, her beauty being of that kind which seems rather to gain than to lose by being worn and sharpened and intensified, she had never appeared so handsome, so grand,. so majestic as now, when passion and jealousy and sin had done their best to disturb and mar her face. Her figure was as upright and unbending as ever; and as she paced there, with long, soft feline steps, she might have passed for any artist's embodiment of some wicked, graceful, dignified, heroine of old- world tragedy. Of what grandeur of crime would not such a creature as this be capable? Nothing Less. than the sublime should she rise to. "Magnificent in sin" like Browning's OW= ; but surely incapable of smaller feminine meannesses, the stab in the dark, the lie which is half a truth, the. smiling sneer, the hinted slander? This struck Sir Lancelot as he stood quietly and watched her, wondering greatly. Immediately she saw him, however, her look changed, and like sun- shine from a thunder-cloud, the gladness over-- Sowed her face and momentarily transformed it from the tragic to the sweet. No suble display, this of histrionic art! She had missed him from, her presence, and behold, the love she thought dead had risen from its ashes, phcenix-like, and burnt within her veins, a living fire. All the years that had come and gone since her first girlish attachment, were as nothing to her • all the ties and barriers between them were shrivelled and destroyed as though they had never existed; and she knew that it was no mere envy of Lady Callerley's position was consuming her ; but a cruel,. pitiless love that had seized upon her soul, and. would not let it go. She made no resistance to this strong passion. Perhaps she knew that at her age, and with her nature, any such resistance would be vain. She gave herself up to it utterly, and lived in. a, sort of dream, in a world peopled only with two persons, Lancelot and herself. All the while she knew that there was no reality in her dream, no possibility of its ever being realised Lancelot did not love her; nay more had they two been the only denizens of that dream world of hers, Lancelot would never have loved her! She recognised this now, and yet it made na difference in her feelings. It was his wife he loved; that same little childish 6ture whom she had once despised as so corn- _ - . ' s.he had
tr I 131:ea,

pletely contemptible a rival ; since grown almost to fear, as possessing reserves of force and fire not at first perceptible. Yes, he loved Silvia! That was evident from the pain any idea of losing her gave to him. Evident from the very fury of jealousy she, Dorothy Breamish, had managed to arouse within him by her subtle hints and insinuations, and the bitter animus he bore towards poor, silly Jack; Jack, who was in reality too honest even for use as a tool. All the wiles and machinations practised had there- fore been so far un,successful. And now! For some weeks she had been con- sullied by a fever of suspense and dread. She knew nothing of what was taking place at Seaton Caller- ley, save what she gleaned from the floating scraps of gossip that travel about from one country house to another. There had been a duet So far, so good. Jack had been severely wounded. Well, that was of no account. Of course he would not have a chance against a Callerley. But why, instead of leaving him upon the field, did Sir Lancelot choose to have his adversary care- fully conveyed to his own home, there to be nursed and coddled by the wife for whose sake these two men had fought? div.p: had been practically starving for months and months together, because whilst it cost a little over 2s. per ton for smelting iron the Marquis of Lonsdale took 6s. for every ton produced. (Cries of " Shame.") Could it to be wondered at that the Workington people were itr suett it—eenciition - -seeing that - thia—great, octopus in the .ehape of an • aristocrat, was sweep- ing away so-large a profit out of • the natural wealth of the country. And you could not possibly dis- sociate the Interests of the miners and ironworkers from those of all the other workeis ef the coutitry ; and be was one who believed in the free fraternisation of industry. He looked forward to the day when the great cause of labour should so far have trtumphed that eVery man Should have work provided for him, and have a good living in return for that work. It seemed strange that in a Christian country where there was more wealth and there were more churches than existed in any other part of the world, there should be hundreds of thousands of men who were willing to work, yet were compelled to starve. However much those who remained outside the ranks of labour organisations might think it was advancing their interests so to remain, their doing so would come home to them and their children who followed them. How,was it possible that in a country where there was a monopply of miaes, of railways, and of machinery, there should be anything else but that of a condition of constant pauperism for a large part of the community? It fell to the lot of nearly one- fifth of the workers of this country to become paupers at one part or other of their lives. Was it right that the men who toiled in the forge or the mills; the factories or the mines, who did the hardest, the most dangerous, and the most disagreeable work, should have the least pay, be the worst clothed, and the worst fed ? Labour as the source of wealth, there- fore all wealth belonged to the labourer, said a great political economist. The workers had to keep them- selves and other people also, for those who did not work for their own living must be living on the labour of some one close. - If payment of members of Parlia- ment could only be brought about, they would clear out the party of lrambugs on both sides of the House, and put in labour representatives who would do something for the working mau. He looked forward to the day when working-men in every trade would be able to exercise their legal andoonstitutional rights to be mem- bers of a trade organisation, which in more than one trade in Warripgton they dared not clo. The speaker,' referring to the subject of the housing of the poorer , classes said he had been in many a town, but in few where the workers were worse housed than in Warring-: ton, and had to pay mere eixtravagant rents. Speaking as one who had had three years' service on a town coun- cil, he said the Warrington ,Corporation had the power to erect artisans' dwellings and let them at low rents, and they could supply as good a dwelling for 3s. a week as es. was now paid for. He believed there was a very . handsome profit on the Warrington Gas Works—that 1 they were a kind of mllcheow. He wanted these profits instead of being divided amongst the rich ratepayers, used for the purpose of • building artisans' dwellings. The speaker concluded by announcing his intention to come to Warrington. to express his opipion on various matters during the nextiocal municipal election. The motion, with MrAitesugas's addition, was put and carried unanimously. Mn. A LICENSING QUESTION AT WARRINGTON. ALDERMAN HARRISON ON BETTING. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, William Green, fruiterer, 1, Leouard-street, applied for the transfer of an off-license from William Taylor, beerseller, 82, Orford Lane.—ln- spector James who took the place of the Chief Constable in his absence, said Mr. Green recently applied for the transfer, when the Chief Constable said he had a good character front Messrs. Rylands for the previous 10 years but was in the habit of attending racing meetings. That was all he had to say against him, or else he was just the man for the position.—Mr. Browne, solicitor, said he appeared for Mr. Green. The only objection raised to the previoue application was that his client was a betting man. There could be no objection in that. He was not a bookmaker and never had been, and he had only attended two race meetings in the present year; and only three in the last 12 menths. How could that posSi- bly affect an outdoor license? His wife proposed to manage the business because he had a shop in Battersby- lane at the present time. If he were going to do any betting he could do so in his own shop. If he had attended races so had other men, and he was afraid some of the very highest gentlemen attended races and betted. Green had a character for 25 years, and Inspector James and Mr. Blunt had known him as a respectable man for a lengtfi of time.—Alderman Flartison said he did not see any objection to the transfer. A man had a right to bet when he liked, if he paid what he lost. Mere was no absolute sin in betting. It was what the highest men in the land indulged in.—Alderman Fran- comb, who was presiding, said he did not see that the fact of a man going to a racecourse could disqualify him for a licence. At the same time, if the police had found that Mr. Green was a bookmaker, he would not be the kind of man to hold a licence. In this case there was ' nothing whatever that could be said in the man's favour, and the licence would be granted.—Alderman Harrison: If Mr. Green does that kind of thing, and applies for a renewai of his licence, it will be considered a very serious matter.—Mr. Browne: I could not expect any other if he became a bookmaker.—The owner of the premises said a pretty sharp look out would be kept on the licensee, and nothing in the nature of bock- making would be tolerated for a minute.

RAILWAY DISASTERS.
WORKMEN'S TRAINS IN COLLISION. FOUR PERSONS KILLED AND MANY INJURED.

A disastrous collision occurred at six o'clock on Tuesday morning, at the Bishopsgate Station of the Great Eastern Railway, between the train leaving Enfield at 5.56 and the 6.4 Walthamstow train. The trains at that hour are almost entirely filled by workmen coming from the populous eastern working class suburbs to their daily work ia Lon- don. The Walthamstow train was standing at the low level new station at Bishopsgate-street at 6.35. Whether the signals were in favour or against the following train, viz., the workmen's train from Enfield, is unknown, but while the Walthamstow train was at a standstill the Enfield train ran down the incline at a sharp pace, crashing into the rear part of the Walthamstow train, the last carriages of which were telescoped by the Enfield engine. The carriages were splintered, and scarcely an occupant in them escaped either death or injury. The scene was heartrending. Numbers pinned in the wrecked carriages were unable to effect their escape, and although scores of willing hands were speedily forthcoming to help, it was a long time before all were extricated. As the dead were brought out they were laid on one side awaiting the police ambulances, and the injured were taken as fast as circumstances would permit to the Lon- don Hospital and to St. Bartholomew's Hospital. A breakdown gang was also promptly on the spot, and by nine o'clock there were few traces of the collision beyond the shatered remnants of the wrecked carriages. Thomas Morgan, who was in the Walthamstow train, states that he was sitting quietly with others when there was a cry that they were being run down, and almost before he could look out of the window there was a great thud, and he fell into the arms of a mate who sat oppo- site. The scene after this, when they scrambled out, Morgan describes as awful. The Enfield train was mak- ing a great noise as if the boiler was about to explode. Then there were screams and cries for help, and as the people were blinded with smoke and steam, the confu- sion was terrible. People shouted at first, but soon realised what had happened, and those who were able set to work to help the less fortunate travellers. There were very few women in either train, but there were a large number of youths going to their early employment, and these seemed to be among the worst sufferers. The following is the list of those killed and injured :

A man, middle-aged, unidentified, now lying at Shore- ditch mortuary. A boy, unidentified, Shoreditch mortuary. John Allen, aged 16, 30, Cambridge-road, Waltham- stow, died at the London Hospital. Walter Jissuney, a middle-aged man, whose head and legs were crushed, also died at this institution.

The adjourned debate on the motion for instruction to Committee on ,National 'Education (Ireland) Bill was resumed by Mr. Sexton who moved an amendment providing for the compulsory acquisition of land for the purposes of residences for the teachers. Mr. Jackson accepted the amendment, and the House then went into Committee on the Bill. A long discussion took Place on an amendment moved by Mr. Sexton with the object of including the schools of the Christian Brothers in the bistitiations to be benefited by the Act. Mr. Sexton aSked for an assurance from the Government that the conscience clause should be made similar to that pre- vailing in 'England and Scotland, and said if that were done the Christian Brethren would be,prepared to accept it, and would 'then become entitled to the Government grant. Mr.. Jackson said he gathered that the Christian Brethren were willing to accept a conscience clause making it,clear that there should beno religious instruc- tion other than that in which parents concurred within the time allotted for secular instruction. Although he could not insist 'on its being done, be would ask the Education Commissioners to consider whether by the adoption of some suctrelause the•schools of the Christian Brethren could not be brought into line with the other schools in thecountry. div.p: MR. AND MRS. GLADSTONE.

Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone arrived at Chester on Monday, and left for London. The Liverpool Congregational Board paid their respects to Mr. Gladstone at Chester., Replying to the right hon. gentleman, the Rev. Mr. Lord, who headed the heputation, said they did not he- lieve in the Ulster Nonconformist manifesto. Mr. Gladstone, being desired by many friends to make speeches or send letters in support of Liberal candidates, writes that it is impossible to accede to these requests severally without the abandonment of other duties im- peratively Incumbent upon him. He assures his corres- pondents, however, that his time and thoughts are incessantly applied in the best mode he can devise for the promotion of their common cause. Mr. Gladstone is to meet a number of the leaders of London Nonconformity at luncheon at the house of the Rev. Guinness Rogers to-day (Saturday.)
THE REV. A. MIIRSELL AT

WARRINGTON. The anniversary of Bold-street Wesleyan Sunday School was held on Sunday, and in connection with it the Rev. A. Mursell of London, preached morning and evening in the 'chapel. The services were well attended, and, it is needless to say, the discourses of Mr. Mursell were highly appreciated. In the afternoon, commencing at half-past two, a sacred cantata, entitled "The Blessing of the Children." was rendered by the choir and scholars. Mr. C. H. Kerry presided, and delivered an interesting address, Special selected hymns were dung at each service by the children, and several anthems were also rendered by the choir, namely, morning, "The Lord is Loving.' evening, " Preserve me, 0 God," and " Send out Thy Light." The solos were taken by members of the choir, Miss Gunton, Miss Fanshawe, and Mr. L. Richardson, being especially deserving of mention. Mr. Peter Harrison was at the organ. The collections for the day amounted to £6O is. 14d.," being," said the Rev. Arthur Mursell, "is. lid. more than the amount the friends had set their minds upon." A very successful anniversary was brought to a close by the singing of the hymn, "Glory to Thee, my God, this night," and pronouncing of the Renedictien. LECTURE ON RUSKIN. On Monday evening, Mr. Mursell gave a lecture in the Bold-st., schoolroom, on "Ruskin, the Man hitnself." Mr. T. Morris presided, and there was a good audience. The Chairman in his opening remarks, having pointed out that Mr. Mursell was one of the oldest .remaining lecturers in the country, said he believed there ,was a good field for young men of the present day, if they would but tax their ingenuity and read and t hink so as to qualify themselves to give of the wealth of their knowledge to the youth of Warrington and other pro- vincial towns. At the present time the Wesleyans of Warrington seemed to be the 'only people who could afford to fetch lecturers to the town; and, in fact,,he felt somewhat ashamed of the institutions of Warring- ton, they seemed to have" goae dead" to such an ex- tent. (Hear, hear.)—The Rev. A. Mursell then gave his lecture which was a highly interesting one. Be remarked that usefulness, and not fame, was the one ambition of Ruskin' s soul. He had been described as "an art critic," but to speak of him simply as such would be like speaking of Socrates as a schoolreaster, or of Cromwell as a farmer. Ruskin was all that was true and beautiful in what went to make an art critic, without any of the sordid side which turned a man into a dealer in art. Closer acquaintance would enhance, and not reduce their respect for Rus- kin. There was a kind of spleen sometimes in his mani- festoes which gave a roughness to the ideal ; but if they approached the bear which looked so grisly at a dis- tance they would find a softness in his eye ; as they drew near they would find it wits no bear at all that hugged them in his Polar grip, but a human brother who clasped them in a love divine. Ruskin had been called a Platonist. If it be Platonism to feel and declare that the true man's mission was not to be ministered unto, but to minister; to turn the fruits of travel, observation, and wealth into unselfish seed with which to sow the acres of the social field, and to declare from public platforms, awl from college chairs that man was not his own, but his brothels keeper, phen 'Ruskin was a Platonist. (Applause) He did his bat to make men true and self-forgetting. He would not abolish railways' or reservoirs, or curtail useful work; he only held the brief on the side of tenderness, honesty, beauty, justice, and truth. He contended for the affinity between natural beauty and moral truth. Referring to the destruction of beautiful scenery, by the promotion of railway and 'ether companies, Mr.. Mursell said that Ruskin saw the soulless crew of dividend hunters turn their blear eyes towards the setting sun, as it met with its " good-night" kiss the ruddy lips of the heather, and the answer they had to give to the serenade of the dying day was a puff from an Havana,. or a spurt of bad tobacco. He saw thick boots stamp °tithe petal of a beautiful flower; vile spades poked through flowery banks; and he knew that in half the instances in which these outrages occurred it was not progress, but pelf that was the moving power. It was but a bubble company, blowing its bubbles in the face of God. These people did not care for progress or for utility, any more than they did for nature or for loveliness. It was because he saw cruelty behind sacri- lege, robbery disguised as enterprise, and trickery visible in the garb of trade that Ruskin rushed like a primt • before the altar, and shook the fist of his anathema at what he could not stay. Ruskin's life was indeed a pro- test against such anomalies. (Loud applause.) • vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Mursell, on the . enotion of Mr. PRIICY SILCOCIC, seconded by Mr. Councillor lititamen, and a similar compliment having been paid to the Chairman, the meeting terminated.

V7I:.LEJO, CALIPQCNIA, TCESDI.2.—The explosion at the Mere Island Navy Yard, which occurred at noon, yesterday, shook this town like an earthquake. It was immediately followed by the ringing of alarm bells in the Nay.y Yard, and when the smoke had cleared away. it was found the expiation had taken place in the shell house of the shell magazine. The burnt and charred bodies (Alton, apprentice seamen were found on the beach two hundred yards from the scene of the explo- sion, and in the midst of the ruins and all around on the hill sides could be seen fre.gments of men's bodies. When the remains were collected it was found that twelve men had bees killed outright. Three, more shockingly Injured, were taken to the hospital in a dying ccrudition. It is not known how the explosion occurred.

div.head: COLLISION Ar LEEDS.
div.p: COLLISION Ar LEEDS.

' An alarming accident occurred at Leeds Midland Railway Station early on Tuesday morning, when the Scotch express due in Leeds from St. Pancras at seven minutes past two came into collision with an engine standing outside the station. It apperrs the engine had left Holbeck about a quarter-past one, and had run down to Leeds Station in Readiness to convey a passenger train from Leeds to Bradford at 2.25. The engine was standing on the line leading to No. 3 platform, and the intention was for the express for Scotland to depart from No. 1 platform. The driver of the stationary engine heard the Scotsman approaching, and looking over the side of his locomotive was terrified to see it coming at high speed direct to the spot where he was standing. He gave the alarm to his fireman, William Hardisty, but neither of them had time either to move the engine or even make good their own escape. In two or three seconds the express crashed with terrific force against the engine. The driver and fireman were both thrown down and about a quarter of a ton of coal fell on Hardisty. The driver was bruised and much cut about the head,but was able to rise and call for assistance to liberate his comrade. The engine of the Scotch express was thrown off the line, and some of the steam tubes throwing off steam added to the confusion and alarm of the passengers. The following were among the injured :—William Hardisty, 25, engine fireman, Beevers-terrace, Beeston-hill, Leeds, thigh scalded and fractured ribs: Jonathan Daniels, 50, engine driver, Barton-terrace, Malvern-road, Beeston- hill, Leeds, scalp wound; Henry Armstrong, 43, corn traveller, Howard-gardens, Cardiff, scalp wound and concussion of the brain; C. H. Cobb, 25, fireman, Bar- ton-terrace, Beeston-hill, Leeds, concussion and scalp wound; William Jackson Dent, 27, Albert-st., Holbeck, railway guard, concussion. After the injuries had been attended to at the infirmary the sufferers were conveyed to their respective destinations with the exception of the fireman Hardisty and Mr. Armstrong, both of whom it was found necessary to detain, but no dangerous results are anticipated. ACCIDENT TO A SCOTCH TRAIN. A serious accident ()enured on Monday night to the 9-5 passenger train from Glasgow and Edinburgh to ; London. When about two miles north of Beatock the driving wheel on the left side of the engine came off and ran into the river Avon, and some of the engine rods dashed into and smashed great holes in the guard's van. The train, however, kept the rails, thereby averting much loss of life.

'S COCOA
A REIL‘RKABLE INCIDENT.

It is a scene in the lecture room of a medical coflege in New Orleans. The professor is lecturing bcfc,re an intelligent class of medical students. He is 6escri bing the human body, its defects and the danger by which it is surrounded. In ordet to illustrate it he has fluids from the human body, which he is subjecting to chemi- cal tests. " Gentlemen," he said, " I have described to you the appearance of the human fluid in a diseased state ; I will now show you how the same fluid appears in a healthy state," and he subjected his own to the test. As he held it up to the light for a moment, his hand trembled, he caught his breath, he paled, and exclaimed , "Gentlemen, I have just made a most horrible dis- covery : I myself have Bright's disease of the kidneys." Well might he be stirred to his inmost depths. He knew that his profession held out no hopes for any per- son in that condition. The !patkies and the 'o/ogies were powerless to save. He was a doomed man accord- ing to them, and, like many a great and valuable life he ! was sacrificed to the tenets of the medical profession. In less than one year lie was dead. The above dramatic and strictly true incident shcws , the terrible danger and mysterious nature of this modern disease, which may well be called the demon of , the present century. It steals into the system like a I thief, manifests its presence by the commonest symp- toms, and fastens itself upon the system before the vic- tim is aware. It is nearly as hereditary as consump- , tion,quite as common,and fully as fatal. Entire families, , inheriting it from their ancestors, have died, yet none of the number knew or realised the mysterious power , which was removing them. Hundreds of people die daily of what is called heart disease, apoplexy, paraly- sis, rheumatism,pneumonia,and other common diseases, ' when in reality it is Bright's disease of the kidneys. These are solemn facts, but all the more serious because of their solemnity. There has never been but one remedy known for the cure of Bright's disease, or even for its relief, and that remedy has become the most popular of all preparations known to the world. It is Warner's SAFE "Cure." It has taken men, and women, too, who were in the lowest stages, and restored them to perfect health and strength. It will invariably check the first stages of this terrible disease, if taken in time. It is endorsed by physicians, approved by scientists, and used by the best people in the land. It is a scientific preparation, and owes its popularity wholly to its power. It can be procured of any reliable dealer.

TION. LIBERALS VERSUS CONSERVATIVES.
A COMPARISON AND A CONTRAST.
BY MAN Lrus.

As I anticipated, ray challenge to the Conservative party to enumerate a list of measures passed mainly or solely in the interests of the working classes by the Conservatives during a certain period as against a list to be presented by myself of such measures passed by the Liberals during an equal period, has not been met in the columns of the "Examiner." An individual signing himself "Conservative," did, it appears from your re. marks the other week, send a reply to my letter, but, instead of meeting the challenge fairly and squarely, he absolutely repeated the very thing which had previously bean done by his party and was the occasion of my throwing out the challenge, in order that a fairer test might be taken ; that is, he advanced in his reply a list of measures passed by Conservative Governments ex- tending over 12 years compared with a list of measures passed during six years Liberal government. Now even taking that basis of comparison, I could have met him and defeated him, as I will presently show, but the fact that his letter was not inserted, because lie did not observe the conditions laid down, would have precluded me iron thus far departing from the terms of my chal- lenge, anxious as I was that he should have an oppor- tunity of making another attempt to meet it in the " Examiner."

As it is, he has chosen to address a reply to the "Observer," and in this communication he has the audacity to claim that in his letter to the " Examiner" he fairly met my challenge, and that it was because it was uaanswerable that it was not inserted. Ile also charges me, apparently unconscious of the nonsense to which he is committing himself with uninanlines s be- cause I did not deal with his letter to the" Examiner ," though, as he himself admitted, it did not appear ! " Conservative," however, in his reply in tilts " Observer " has come to something more like the point than formerly. lie advances two lists of measures, Con_ servative and Liberal respectively, for equal periods, and thus far meets the case. But he places them under this heading :—" Lite of measures passed solely or mainly in the interests of the working-classes from 1888 to 1891,, yet while he commences the Conservative list in 1886 and finishes it in 1891, he commences the Liberal list in 1880 and finishes it in 1884. " Conservative " in this way shows that his heading is inaccurate, and furnishes another example of his propensity for mendacity and trickiness, for the Liberals were in office from April 1880 to August 1885, add by finishing at 1884 he either means to pre- sent only five years' Liberal against•stx years' Conserva- tive legislation, or he implies that tile Liberals did nothing in 1885, which,as will be seen later on, was very far from being the case. Below will be found the list I have to advance in contradistinction to his. The Lineral measures mentioned by me I place in chronological order, according to the years in which they were passed, but I have indicated by an asterisk the ten Liberal Bills he men- tions, so that my readers may see exactly what lie has and what he has not omitted in his Liberal list. This list I give exactly as it stands in the " Observer,' where the measures contained in it are not mentioned in order according to date. •

Now, Sir, I think I have furnished a complete answer to " Conservative." I have adduced 80 measures, nearly three times his number. I have thus answered also the Conservative placard and circular which have been published in Warrington claiming BO working class measures for the 12 years' of office the Conservatives had during 1874-91 ; because I have shown that the Liberalfi passed 20 more working-class measures in their six, than the Tories did in their twelve years. If I were to enter into the question of how many working-class mea- sures passed during Conservative administration were carried by the Liberal advocacy and the Liberal vote, I could enlarge my list and reduce "Conservative's." There is the Free Education Bill of 1891, included in " Conservative's " list, for instance. It is well known that that Act was carried by the votes of the Liberal members—more Tories voting against it than for it. Then he claims the Technical Instruction Act, of 1891, which even in the Conservative circular and placard is credited to the Liberals, though passed while the Conservatives were in office. I might further descant on the moral worth of one such naeasure as the County Franchise Act, passed by the Liberals, as com- pared with a host of minor measures passed by the Conservatives ; and upon the fact that the Conserva- tives, being last in office, have had the advantage of a more advanced public opinion in their favour to aid them in doing the little they have done, in the past six years for the working-man, which points have already been dealt with isy another correspoadent. But Ido not now propose to enter into discussion of these points. lam content to leave matters as they at pre- sent stand, not indeed, with the slightest hope that " Conservative " or his party will admit their defeat, as such a thing is inconceivable, but with perfect confi- dence as to what will be the verdict of imps rtial work.. ing-class electors. ‘Varrington, June 15th, 1892.

T ON Monday Mr. Berarourt,as leader Dissoih;io of the House of Commons, made n* his promised statement with regard to the impending dissolution. It was thought that his announcement would settle everything, k but it is CO indefinite that in some respects it I 44/es matters as much unsettled as before. All 11 that Mr. Balfour can be got to say is that the thssolution is "very unlikely to take place before the end of the week beginning on Sunday, the 19th 6f June, and it is not unlikely to occur after the kiddie of tho week beginning on the 20th." From this it will be seen that Parliament may be dis- 401ved on Saturday the 25th June, or the dissolu- tion may be delayed to the Tuesday or Wednesday following. It is thought that the Tories favour the later date with the idea of preventing the _i!tilk of the elections being fixed on a Satur- -7,a3', which is the most :convenient day for tile working classes. The party that opposed .83 I°lls as they could the franchise be- -I.ng given to the masses would, of course, be act- ing in harmony with their traditions if they des- tob a party trick to prevent the franchise „Ing exercised:to its fullest extent. So far as :arrington is concerned, it may happen that the ,"tion will take place on the Saturday or Mon- day following Walking Day, whilst the bulk of the Workers are taking a brief holiday. This would be int,°at unfortunate, for it would mean that some of ne electors would be away on various excursions ell the day of polling, and they would be put in the raition of having either to curtail their holiday or te"o the exercise of the franchise. The Mayor, lin ieturning Officer, will doubtless have this in itici in fixing the day, and will, it is to be hoped, s7'3 Counsel with the representatives of both poll- 'cal Parties before deciding. With regard to Parliament itself, there is no %son why it should not receive its death son- htee en the 24th or 25th instant, for there is it:: Measure of moment to be passed. As to the ti:811 Local Government Bill, the course taken is e one we have for some tine anticipated— is to say, it is not to be passed at all. In it is already withdrawn ; but we may be :lire it will be dangled bE-fore the electors as -oraething the Tories propose to give if they are . 41.4. nted a new lease of power. But tl.te trick is 1.:11rely stale by this. The very measure which withdrawn was promised at the last oieet. it has been promised year after year now, after the Tories have been in office six Ywenra, it is being promised again! Electors who 4 el.' in doubt in 1885 and DM can have no doubt They had some reason to think that it 1714 perhaps be worth while to give the Tories „W °PPortunity of carrying out what they then °elaimed as their policy, na:nely, " equal laws,' :11tici "no coercion." They have had the opportun- eoeY, and they have abused it. Instead of "no it ,reimi," Ireland is at present subject to the most ' I.ingent Coercion Act that she has over known ; While the phrase " equal laws" has become a by wobnrcl and a reproach. The fact is, the Tories R tamed office under false pretences: and the time e Close at hand when they will have to face the :eters they have so basely betrayed. They . .Mlot plead that the opportunity has not been !. ren them of passing a Local Government Bill or Ireland ; the delay is of their own making; 4:1, it must not be forgotten that they have to Wasted the time of Parliament by trying lan Provide compensation to brewers. That was thi3Plrt of their programme, and,further,the y took thni Course in defiance of the expressed desire of the People as demonstrated by public meetings , runghout the country. Indeed, it is not too intilla,h to say that there never was a Government So shamelessly disregarded their pledges, and it can with the strictest truth be said I thatC they have done the things they ought not to 1, t4n),e done, and left undone the things they ought _ nlive done, and there is no health in them.

div.head: "TOUCLE AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCLE AND GO."
HORATIO OGDEN.—Your letter will appear in our next ivsue.

The Tories profess to be quite shocked at Mr. Gladstone "sitting on the fence," as they call it, on the eight hours question. He is, at any rate, in a better position than Lord Salisbury, who is where he always has been—on the wrong side of the fence.

"Slaves cannot breathe in England," says the poet, but the poet is given over to Fancy rather than to Fact. They breathe at Bolton, where as tram-men they have had to strike in their effort to secure one day off in fourteen! They ought to be helped by the public in fighting this battle, and hold out until they have one day in seven which they can call their own.

Mr. Gladstone has declined to commit the Liberal party, at the last moment, to Home Rule for Scotland. Seeing that it has not as yet had the sanction of the National Liberal Federation, the decision is a wise one. There is a time for everything; and the time for Home Rule for Scot- land, as well as for England and for Wales, will come when Home Rule has been proved to be a good thing for Ireland.

The Liberal canvass promises exceeding well for the return of Dr. Houston for Warrington, and nobody knows this better than the Tories. They find it difficult to get volunteer canvassers, and are driven to rely, to a large extent, upon their agent. But Mr. }Tampon is the paid ser- vant of the party, and,when he canvasses, does he not become a paid canvasser? This is sailing very near the wind; but the Tories will do it when they are in a difficulty.

There was a very general expression of regret at the meeting of Parr's BankiNg 'Jo., Limited, on Tuesday, on the retirement of Mr. J. Charlton Parr, from the position of chairman, after a ser- vice of 18 years. Liberals who know how the wind was blowing over the Conservative field, a few months since, may find satisfaction in the fact that Mr. Parr is not employing his well-earned leisure as Tory candidate for Warrington. He would have been a very strong opponent ; while the present candidate, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, is, by comparison, undoubtedly much" below Parr."

The rumour is abroad in Warrington that Waiking Day has been altered again in conse- quence of the General Election, but this is not so. It is too late to consider such a course even if it were desirable ; and the processions will therefore be held on Friday week, the Ist of July. It is not known as yet with certainty, when the Dissolution will take place. The Tory Government are try- ing to scheme things so that the elections cannot be held on a Saturday. They are "the friends of the working-man," of course ; but they would show their friendship by avoiding the working- man's day.

The Tories are making the most of the Manifesto of the Ulster Nonconformists ; but it will not disturb any Nonconformist in this country who has watched the Home Rule movement. One sentence runs :—" We believe that no guarantees, moral or material, can be devised which will guard the rights of the Protestant minorities which are scattered throughout Ireland against the encroach- ments of a Roman Catholic majority endowed with legislative and executive powers, and thus directed by their clergy."

This is the language of timidity accustomed to ascendancy. What of the " scattered Protestant minorities" in Ireland at the present moment P Do they suffer from attacks of the Catholics by whom they are surrounded 1 Not a bit of it. Mr. Pierce Mahony, a Protestant, returned to Parliament by Catholic votes, testified to that when in Warrington, and his testimony is sup- ported by the experience of Protestanta in the South of Ireland.

Real dangers should be met and provided for but it is no use wasting time over imaginary dan- gers. Touching this view of things, Emerson quotes a Persian proverb which runs, in the trans- lation, as follows :
Somv of your griefs you have cured, And others you still lia7e survived ; But what moments ot pain you've endured From evils that never arrived.

As will he seen from the letters which we pub- lish in another column, Dr. Houston has carried the war into the enemy's camp. He has written to the Duke of Abercorn personally, and supported his communication by a copy of his letter to the "Irish News." It will give the Ulster Convention something to think about,for it furnishes an array of facts which are not to be gainsaid—facts which prove to demonstration that the Roman Catholics of Ireland have for many years set a noble ex- ample in toleration by returning Protestants to Parliament.

-- People who are still anxious as to this side of the Home Rule question should read Mr. John Morley's speech at Plymouth on Tuesday. Here is an extract which shows that the people of Ire- land can and do act independently in matters political. Mr. Morley says:— In the year 1874 the Archbishop of Tuatn, *so was the most influential prelate of this century, and a friend and colleague of that great patriot Daniel O'Connell and the priests, opposed Mr. O'Connor Power; yet the Catholic voters elected him by an immense majority. In 1880, the late Mr. Parnell .(cheers) stood for Mayo and Cork, in both eases against an ecclesiastical candidate. In 1880, in Roscommon, the bishops and priests supported The O'Connor Don; and the people—all Catholics— threw him over. In 1883, there was a Papal rescript against the Parnell testimonial, forbidding a collec- tion to be made at the church doors, and all the bishops and the priests were ordered to discounten- ance the testimonial in every way. I have heard, from very good authorities, that the only effect of that rescript was that a fund which otherwise would have been £20,000 rose to £40,000.

It is just as we expected—the Tories, taking their cue from Lord Salisbury's speech, are trying to make it out that trade would be wonderfully im- proved undei a system of Protection. But, if this be the case, how comes it that a Tory. Government has been in office for six years, and failed to improve trade by giving this Protection? Is it a good reason for again placing them in power that they have known what to do and wouldn't do it ? If there was anything in the Tory talk about Fair Trade,this negligence would constitute the strongest argument against the present Government: But there isn't ; it means just as much and just as little as it meant before the last General Election, and, as the result shows, it meant nothing.

Has Alderman Harrison been in a jocular mood again—or what? The other week he distinguished himself by an extraordinary deliverance on the subject of drunkenness ; and, on Monday morning, speaking again from the Warrington bench, he told the world what he thinks aboutbetting. He said :—" A man had a right to bet, provided he oould pay when he lost. There was no wrong in it. It was what the highest in the land did."

Holding these views' the oratorical Alderman should have proceeded to explain, if he could, why the legislature has passed Acts of Parliament to put down betting ; and why in a later case, the same day,he did not encourage the boys wiva were brought before him for playing cards, instead of fining them half-a-crown each. Lie might of course say that it is his business to administer—not to make the law; but it has happened before now that he has declined to administer what he regarded as a bad law.

Perhaps the explanation is to be found in the fact that these boys were not of that ever-to-he- adored class known a " the highest in the land." A good set phrase, as old Polonius would say, with a fine and unmistakeable Tory flavour. Why not add to the decalogue—" Thou shall regulate thy conduct by that of the highest in the land P" And yet these vulgar street boys might plead, remem-

div.head: MAD TUROUOR DRINK AT RUNCORN.
div.p: MAD TUROUOR DRINK AT RUNCORN.

Before Mr. Brundrit , at Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, James Hooley, of Liverpool, was charged with wandering abroad at Halton, supposed to be of unsound mind. Superintendent Atherton said the man was locked up for his own safety. The prisoner said he was out of his mind through drink. He had already been in Rainhill Asylum on two occasions after drinking bouts. He could not leave beer alone.—He was dis- charged on promising to leave the town, and he was escorted to the extremity of the town. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the magis- trates imposed a fine of 103., including costs, upon the following employes of the Ship Canal Company, at Norton :—Frederick Wright, John Holloway, Jas. John- son, Thomas Heslop, and Frederick Baker. Wright said he had borrowed the dog because his hut was infested with rats, and Superintendent Atherton observed that there were also plenty of rabbits in the locality.—Roger Tickle, of Aston-by-Sutton, was also fined 10s., including costs, for keeping a dog without a license.

Albert Peck, a s.,ldier on the reserve, sorl'oi;Liormer local cab proprietor, was again brought up at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, charged with stealing a coat in September last from the shop of Mr. Marsh, pawn- broker, Church-street. It appeared that the defendant would lose his deferred pay of ed. a day if he were con- vinted,and as the Beach thought this would he too severe a punishment for kis first offence, and as he had been in custody for several days, they discharged him, with a skivere caution.

Our readers will be pleased to learn that improved postal arrangements came into operation on Monday in the Widnes district. Formerly the last collection of letters was at 8.25 p.m.. and by payment of an addi- tional halfpenny, at 8-30 p.m. Under the new regula- tions, however, letters can he posted at the general office until ten p.m.. and 10.10 p.m. for the extra half- penny, and letters for Runcorn can be posted up to five a.m. At the receiving offices the time of the last collec- tion will he extended as follows:—Mersey-road, 9.5 p.m. Sim ms' Cross, 9.5 p.m. ; Halton View, 8 50 p.m. : and Appleton Village, 3,35 p.m. The despatches will remain- as at present. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, John Powell applied for permission to sell at the Albion Inn, Nelson- street, under the lictpse lately held by John Massey.— Superintendent Atherton said the license of this house was absolutely gone. The holder of the license was con- victed of felony at the last Daresbury Petty Sessions. This person now applied for temporary authority until next licensing day, and it was for the Bench to say whether the house was ever to be licensed again or not. In reply to questions, Powell said he applied oa his own behalf.—Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, who had previously acted for the owners of the house,said he had no instruc- tions to do so on that cccasioa.—Mr. James Reynolds said the Bench must have more information before they dealt with the matter—The owners are Ann and Esther Massey. JOSEPH PRITCHARD'S sale shop is 51,High-st.. his workshop 4, Bridge-st.—Advt.
A RUNCORN TRADESMAN AND HIS WHITSUNTIDE STALL.

Jabez Horrocks, newsagent, High-st., was summoned to Runcorn Police Court on Monday to answer a charge of obstructing Penketh-lane on Whit Monday by erecting a stall there.—P.S. Woolley said the stall caused the street to be completely blocked all day, and two con- stables had to be stationed there to keep the people moving.—Mrs. Horrocks said she would sooner he sum- moned than take the stall down, and defendant also refused to remove it.—The defendant contended that he had a perfect right to erect the stall there, as it did not project beyond the steps leading to his sh.op. They had erected a stall there for years,and no complaint had been previously made. They had as much right to make a bit on Whit Monday as strangers.—Superintendent Atherton : On the fair ground.—Defendant : And at the shop.—The magistrates informed the defendant that he had no right to obstruct the highway and ought to have obliged the police. As this was the first offence, a fine of 18, and costs 108, would be imposed.

There is now displaced in the shop window of Mr. U. Bellannv, Examiner Office, High-street, a portrait in oils of the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, pastor of St. Edwards Catholic Church. The portrait, which is from the brush of Signor A. F. D'Cavallaro, is a life size half-bust, and the likeness is an admirable one. The artist this most happily caught the worthy doctor's expression, and the colouring and general finish of the painting are excellent. The portrait is a present to Dr. Gastaldi from the;artist, who is now engaged in the painting of a repressntation of the Virgin in the Chapel of our Lady.

ACTION BY A WIDNES CAD PROPRIETOR.

Yesteraay, at Widnes County Court,before his Honour Judge Shand, James H. Lea, cab proprietor, Victoria- road, sued Messrs. S. Cowburn and Sons, contractors, of Wigan for £lO damages caused to a brougham through the defendsint's negligence. Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. C. H. Lewin defended. On the first January of this year the defendants were con- structing Market-st., and it was alleged that on the evening of that date boles and heaps of rubbish were left, without either lamps burning or a watchman to warn people not to enter the street. The plaintiff's car- riage ran into one of these boles and the axles were broken, the front part of the cab knocked in, and the window smashed.—For the defence it was contended that the accident would not have happened had ordin- ary care been used and witnesses were called to prove that the driver of the conveyance was under the influ- ence of drink and was driving at a rapid rate, which the occupants of the vehicle could not prevail upon him to moderate.—Judgment was given for the defendant. A FISHMONGERS' QUARREL AT RUNCORN.

On Monday at Rutmorn Police Court, George Duckett. Wm. Green, Frederick Chell, and John Salt, fish dealers and fish hawkers, were summoned for creating a breach of the peace in Church-st., on the 2nd June. P.C. Booth deposed that all the defendants were fighting on the" floor "near the Rose anel Crown. Duckett told the Bench that ever since he married Salt's sister eighteen months ago he had been continually annoyed by Salt and Chell. On the day in question Salt came and said "You can thank me for fetching your wife's watch out of pawn," and Duckett replied " I paid a pound to get you out of trouble, and that will cover the watch if ever you did such a thing." Salt then struck at him and they closed together. Chell then came and attacked him, but his assistant Green kept him off.—Chell said Duckett made a regular practice of sendinz: his men to thrash him and Salt.—Sat handed up a letter to explain his share in the matter.—Mr. Reynolds said it was a dis- graceful and disagreeable way in which these people lived together, and bound them all over to keep the peace for six months each, they to pay 9s. 61. costs. On Thursday afternoon there was a large assembly in Runcorn Parish Church to witness the marriage of Mr. Charles Henderson Harrison, of The !lollies, Runcorn, to Miss Beatrice Ellen Banks, of Weston House, Runcorn, daughter of the late Mr. William Bank., JP. The bride, who was given away by her brother, Mr. William Banks, was attired in an ivory brocaded silk dress, with long train, and she wore a tulle veil with orange blossoms, and in her hand carried a beautiful bouquet the gift of the bridegroom. She was attended by Miss Georgie, Miss Eunnie, and Miss Daisy Banks (sisters) and Miss Elsie Leak (niece of the bridegroom) and they were all charm- ingly attired, the two former in dresses of detain° with green ribbon and white lace and the latter in cream surah silk frocks, with lace hats to match. They each wore an ornament, the gift of the bridegroom. Mr. A. Harrison, brother of the bridegroom, officiated as best man. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, vicar of Runcorn, and the Rev. G. H. Kingston (curate in charge of Weston). After the usual formalities had been gone through, the wedding party left the sacred edifice, to the strains of Afendelssohn's Wedding March, played on the organ by Mr. Johnson. An " at home " was held at Weston House, about 50 guests being present,and in the evening a select party of friends celebrated the occasion. The members of Weston Cricket Club were also entertained in the afternoon. Mr. and Mrs. Harrison departed in the afternoon for Windermere. The presents were very numerous and valuable.

The local secretary of the Royal Manchester, Li y- e rpool, Agricultural Society, at a ria.ptiniz, re- ported that the fund in connection with the forth- coming show now stands at £1,275. DARRSBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.

At a special meeting of the Daresbury Highway Board, held in the Board-room. Daresbury, on Tues- day afternoon, there were present Mr. Joseph Cliffe (in the chair), and a moderate attendance of members. The Foot Hill Road Committee reported that they had read Messrs. Brunner and Co.'s reply in the negative to the resolution passed at the last meeting, and were unanimous that the Board should re-consider the matter. Considering the liberality of the company in giving laud, diverting the watercourses, erecting new fences on both sides of the road, placing material close at hand for the filling up, and giving ..£6O towards the cost of the work, they (the Committee) recommended that the Board accept their offer, and carry out the work in accordance with the plan and specification. After some discussion, it was resolved unanimously that the report of the committee be accepted and adopted by the Board. COLLIERY FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.

On Friday morning John Thompson, aged about twenty-eight years, who was better known as John Toplass, was killed in the Deep Pit of the St. Helens Collieries Company. Deceased was em- ployed as a labourer. He was walking behind a "journey" of boxes of stuff, which was in charge of a pony lad named John Price, when the last wagon by some means got off the rails. Deceased was as- sisting the lad to put the box on the rails again, when the pony started, and the corner of the wagon caught deceased in the region of the heart, and crushed him against the roof. The lad went for help, but deceased succumbed a few minutes afterwards. The body was taken to his lodgings in Rigby-st. An inquest was held at the Town Hal!, on Monday morning, before Mr. Jones, the deputy- coroner. Mr.Hall,her Majesty's Inspector of Mines, was present, and Mr. J. 0. Swift, represented the colliery company, whose agent, Mr. F. France was also present. After hearing the evidence, the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

div.head: SUN INSURANCE OFFICE.
div.p: SUN INSURANCE OFFICE.

We have to band the report of the ahove-named office, for the year ended December 31st, 1891. From this we glean the following facts :—The premiums received, less re-insurances, for the year, amount to £957,33245. 2d., an increase of £85,053 2s. over those of the preceding year. The total sums in- sured after deduction of amounts re-insured, amounted to .£373,716,110, an increase of £12,238,490, over the corresponding figures for the previous pear. The income from investments dur- ing the year has amounted to £69,250 14s. 5d., and after providing for the usual reserve of 40 per cent. of the premiums to cover liabilities under current policies, a profit of £130,321 Cs. 11d, has been realised. The balance on profit and loss account has been increased to £194,194 18s. 4d. Out of this an interim dividend of £5 on each old share was paid last January ; and the Directors have declared a further dividend of the equivalent amount, 2s. on each new share, and a bonus of 4s. 61, on each new share.
