div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
IT RUNCORN, dm.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The negotiations which have been commenced by the Runcorn Commissioners with a view to the purchase of the Waterworks meet with the almost universal approval of the ratepayers. The water supply of every town should be in the hands of the 'ocal authority, and it is a pity that steps were net taken sears ago to acquire the waterworks, when probably a much less price would have sufficed.
Mr. Frank Wiswall was unanimously elected chairman if Runcorn Board of Commissioners, on Weelnesday, in succession to Mr. 11. J. Grice. May success attend his year of office

The proposal to hokl the election of Runcorn Guardians triennially instead of annually should receive the assent of the ratepayets by an over- whelming majority when the poll is taken in October. The system works well in other Unions, and is besides a saving of time end trouble, and of pecuniary advantage.

Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., has spent a busy time in the division this w:ek. He has visited almost every part of it, and had interviews with those who are working to secure his return. Last night there was a meeting in Union Hall at Runcorn, and Mr. Brunner was present. The proceedings were private. By the way, I observed that Mr. Brunner gave his usual subscription of one guinea to the fund for giving the workhouse children a seaside trip.
Mr. W hiteley has visited Runcorn twice this week. On Thursday evening he addressed a private meeting of his supporters in Runcorn, and gave them eome advice as to the conducting of the election.

In Widnes Division Mr. J. S. Gilliat,the Conserva- tive candidate, has held a public meeting each evening during the week. He is by no means a finished speaker, and from what I hear he has failed to arouse any enthusiasm. Mr. J. Wnite, one of his prominent supporters, appeared to have lost his temper at the Widnes meeting on Tuesday, and made a personal attack en Mr. Shores, the Liberal agent, Is this an indication that having lost Mr. Moss, they are afraid they will lose a seat,and have taken to abusive personalities to keep their spirits up?

div.head: RUNCORN DROWNING MYSTERY.
div.p: THE RUNCORN DROWNING MYSTERY.

Yesterday afternoon the adjourned inquiry into the circumstances of the death of Sarah Ann Street, who was drowned in the Bridgewater Canal at Runcorn, at midnight on Whit Wednes- day, was held in the Police Court. Superintendent Atherton said they had only obtained one addi- tional witness, and he was called—Jas. Clark, 24, Jack- son-st., here deposed that he was awakened by screams, and be threw up the bedroom window. fie heard a man say "Oh dear dear, she is going down." Witness shouted" Why don't you get in or give her some assis- tance ?" and the man replied that he could not swim. Witness then saw other persons come on the canal bank, and he saw the body recovered. His house was on the wpposite side of the canal.— The Coroner, in summing up, said the fact that the prisoner had told several different stories of the affair, was ground for the gravest suspicion. He suggested that an open verdict should be returned, so that it would leave the police free to further investigate the matter ; and the jury returned a verdict of " Found ' drowned." Mr. Rogerson, the foreman, said it was the wish of the jury that the Coroner should severely cen- sure the prisoner for not attempting to rescue the woman when he was on the bank.—The Coroner said he could not accede to that request.

div.head: BRFORE: Tif H BECK.
div.p: BRFORE: Tif H BECK.

Subsequently the prisoner was brought before Mr. J. Handley.. The evidence previously reported was re- neated,and the magistrates ordered his discharge, on the ground that there was not a prima facie charge.

TUE ULSTER CONVENTION.
LETTER FROM DR. HOUSTON TO THE DUKE
OF ABERCORN. 52, Fitzwilliam Square, Dublin. June 15, 1692.

div.head: My Lord Duke, _ . .
div.p: My Lord Duke, _ . .

I beg leave to enclose for your perusal and considera- tion copies of two letters, one addressed by me to the Dublin" Daily express," and the other to the (Belfast) " Irish News.' The facts stated in these letters are indisputable : the arguments based upon those facts you will find to be unanswerable.

It will be for you, and all other persons responsible for the summoning of the Ulster Convention, and for its action, and the consequences of that action, to recon- cile your conduct with those facts and the conclusions that inevitably follow from them. It will not be enough to point to ether times, when every church persecuted those that differed from its doctrines ; when Roman Catholic persecuted Protestant, and when Churchman persecuted Roman Catholic and Dissenters with edify- ing impartiality. We are not living in those times ; we are living in the last decade of the nineteenth century. Neither will it be enough to point to other countries. We are living in Ireland, and the Irish Roman Catholics have never been persecutors. " The children of martyrs never are," as Cardinal Manning has finely put it. As to Boycotting and the Plan of Campaign, except perhaps that they have been condemned by that exalted Ecclesiastic, for whose eternal perdition the devout Orangeman so frequently and fervently, and withal so tersely, prays. They have, of course, nothing to do with Roman Catholicism.
I need not pursue the subject. farther, Your Grace's

great intelligence, and a liberal education, will preserve you from falling into that confusmn of ideas engendered , by the fact that, in our unhappy country, untoward circumstances have conspired to drive the Roman Catholics into one political camp, and the Protestants— especially Churchmen—into anothar. Toleration is the heritage of the Irish Catholics of to-day. They are entitled to point to the record of their past and ask : " Why are we to be suspected of intentions so inconsist- ent with our conduct in former times." Is it to be sup- posed that the restoration to them—and us—of those liberties of which we were both despoiled by the unblushing bribery and shameless corruption of Pitt, will suddenly convert them from kindly and tolerant citizens to brutal and bigoted persecutors ? What warrant is there for so wounding a presumption? Nemo repente fit turpissimus is good sense as well as good Latin.

I observe that the proceedings are to be commenced with some pious exercises. Might I be allowed to sug- gest, asa useful addition to the programme, a short discourse on the text," Judge not that ye be not judged," in its application to political opponents ? I have the honour to be

div.head: Your Grace's Obedient Servant, ARTHUR HOUSTON. The Most Noble The Duke of Abercorn. ---- " NATIONALIST LIBERALITY,"
div.p: Your Grace's Obedient Servant, ARTHUR HOUSTON. The Most Noble The Duke of Abercorn. ---- " NATIONALIST LIBERALITY,"
The following is the Communication referred to by Dr. Houston, as addressed by him to the editor of the " Irish News."

Sir,—As I perceive that you considered my letters addressed to the " Daily Express," under the above heading, important enough to be referred to in a lead- ing article, lam encouraged to ask you to allow me to enlarge in your columns upon another branch of the subject.

The impending" convention "owes its existence to the assertion that, under a native Parliment, the Pro- testant minority will be delivered over bound hand and foot, to the Catholic majority. Now, this assertion assumes that constituencies containing a majority of Catholic voters will return exclusively Catholic repre_ sentatives, and that as in any conceivable disturbance of seats, such constituencies must largely outnumber those in which the Protestant voters would be in a majority, a native Parliment would be an essentially Catholic body. Judging from the past conduct of the Catholic voters of Ireland, there is not a shadow of foundation for this assumption. On the contrary, the Catholics of Ireland have been generous to imprudence in electing Protestants to represent them. Anyone who wishes to learn the extent to which this practice his prevailed will find much valuable information collected in a lecture deliver- ed in 1886 by Mr. Charles Dawson, ex-Lord Mayor of Dublin and ex-M.P. for Carlow, which was published by the Irish Press Agency. Here are some of the facts In the general election of 1832, thirty-three over- whelmingly Catholic constituencies used their newly- acquired power to return forty-three Protestant members of Parliament! Among these were Mr. Ruthven, the colleague of O'Connell in the city of Dublin ; Mr. Mullins, a cousin to Lord Ventry, the Colleague of O'Connell's son-in-law in the county of Kerry ; the Hon. Pierce But- ler, brother of the Earl of Kilkenny, in the county of Kilkenny; the Hon. Wm. Parsons, eldest son of the Earl of Rossi, in the King's County ; the brother of Lord Clare and the son and heir of Lord Guillamore, in the county of Limerick ; Mr. (afterwards Sir) David Roche, in the eityof Limerick ; Henry Grattan and his brother in the counties of Meath and Wicklow ; Sir Charles Henry Coote, in the Queen's County ; Mr. Talbot, grandson of Lady Talbot de Malallide, in Athlone ; The Hon George Lambe, brother of Lord Melbourne, and a connection of Under-Secretary Drummond, in Dungarvon. Again, in 1848, no less than forty Protestants were returned by Catholic constituencies; and in the bye elec- tions from 1848 to 1868, many striking instances oi religious toleration occurred, such as at Limerick, where Mr. Ball, a Catholic, was rejected, and Mr. Jas. Spaight, a Protestant, returned. At the general election of 1868, thirty-three Protestants were elected by Catholic constituencies, and these includ- ed, as before, many members of the aristocracy, such as Lord Bourke, Lord St. Laurence, and Lord Otho Fitz- gerald. The Catholics had not yet learned the folly of returning Conservatives, and sent Tories of even the pronounced type of Colonel Vandeleur to represent them. Among other non-Catholics returned by Catholic con- stituencies at this election were Chichester Fortescue, Charles White, Mr. Whitworth, and Mr. Pim, the last mentioned of whom was the colleague of the Tory Pro- testant, Sir Arthur Guinness, now Lord Ardilaun. From the foregoing facts,it is manifest that the Catho- lic eles.t.s:- c Ir land did not regard the religion of the candidate for their suffra.ges at all, and paid much less attention to his political oponions than might have been expected, though this latter consideration gradually ac- quired more influence, and ultimately, at the election of 1374, when the question of Home Rule began to develop, the political opinions of the candidates became the deter- mining consideration with the Catholic electorate. The result was a diminution in the number of non-Catholic members returned by Catholic constituencies. But this was caused by the paucity of Protestant candidates who adopted the national demand. Any Protestant who did so was received with open arms, and 28 Protestants were returned by Catholic constituencies, including Isaac Butt, William Shaw, Jesepli G. Biggar, and Charles Stewart Parnell.

To bring the record down to the present time, there are, I believe, some dozen Protestant members of Parlia- ment returned by Irish Nationalist and Catholic consti- tuencies. I need not go through the list, but I may be permi- ed to point out that Ulster contributes its quota to the n,..aber. Mr. Thomas A.Dickson is an Ukter Presbyter- ian ; yet as in former times he was returned by Catholic VOtt.S. SO at the last election he was returned by a Catho- lic constituency for the St. Stephen's Green Division of Dublin. The town of Galway, the city of the Tribes— that intensely Catholic constituency, in which at the last contested election only 162 Tories, not to say Protes- tants, mustered at the poll—is represented by a Bally- money Presbyte, ian, Mr. Pinkerton. One of the members for Cavan County is Mr. Knox, a Protestant ; the other is Mr. Thomas O'Hanlon. But mark. A con- vention was held only the other day in his constituency. The Catholic clergy, as well as the Catholic laity, at that convention selected a Belfast Protestant—Mr. Young— to oppose the Catholic—Mr. O'Hanlon— at the coining election, because they differ from Mr. O'llanlon on the unfortunate controversy which is now dividing the Nationalist party. The very same thing occurred, on the same day, when Mr. Jeremiah Jordan, an Ulster Methodist, was selected to contest Mr. Wm. Redmond s seat in North Fermanagh. It would be superfluous to multiply instances of the application by the flesh Catho- lic voter of the great principle that in political matters a man's religion is not to be regarded. If the Catho- lic voters err at all, they err on the other side ; they are anxious to recognise, and quick to trust and honour, any Protestant who shows a disposition to meet them in a friendly and sympathetic spirit. They remem- plunderin.g their Protestant fellow- ber the heroic sacrifices made., and. the splendid service rendered by Protestant patriots in. the. long struggle NaVnidiat reason is. there for apprehending turollpeot inions are in oppressing constituencies. will cease to elect as their now, it is Co be hoped, approaching its termination. harmony with their own? And Why. then, I ask, are the Osth. alms of. Ireland to be ac- cused of a sinister and nefarious dee. ign of persecuting rcat oni pau rtr cpoliticalreyan if they elect them in such a proportion as from the ' history of the past, we are entitled to antici pa,te, and if the Protestant constituencies choose to adhere to the practice of electing Protestant representatives why mav we net have an Irish House of Commons in 'which the insjoriiy of the members shall be Protestants? It would then be the Catholic majority that would be delivered over to the Protestant minority ! I commend these facts, and these figures, and these arguments, to the attentive consideration of every fair- minded and reflecting man and woman who either takes part in the proceedings of the convention or attends its meetings. Let the speakers explain them away if they ttan. I shall take care that they are brought to the notice of some of those who will come forward to preach the false gospel of distrust and dread, including some of

the Catholics who are to countenance by their presence the foul calumny on their co-religionists. I do not envy ' these latter gentlemen their feelings when they are per- forminr, that hateful task. Ireland will not soon forget that when Catholic Nationalists were holding out the right hand of friendship to their Protestant fellow- countrymen, and asking them to join in building up a united, and tkerefore prosperous, contented, and loya nation, some recreant Catholics were to be found ready to whisper in the ear of their Protestant friends that Catholic was not to be trusted.—Yours faithfully, ARTHUR HOUSTON.
52, Fitzwilliam Square. Dublin, 11th June, 1892.

Commenting on the above, the" Irish News' says We publish elsewhere a highly interesting letter from Dr. Arthur Houston, Q.C., which we commend to the care- ful perusal of our conventionist friends, and especially those of them who are wont to prate of Catholic intoler- ance. Dr. Houston is himself a Protestant,whose views, as he has told us, nave been considerably broadened by studying facts in regard to his Catholic fellow-country- men, instead of adopting the random statements and sharing the groundless fears, either experienced or assumed, of purblind bigots. Dr. Houston adduces ample evidence of the toleration and liberality of Cathe lice in the past, and what he relies on is not mere hearsay evidence, but is borne out by history. The" Unionist " who can read Dr. Houston's letter without feeling ashamed of himself is surely fit for " treasons, strata- gems, and spoils."

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting -of-171-e-inenaTiers of Runcorn Board of Commissioners was held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday. Mr. H. J. Grice presided and there were present Messrs. Fisher, Pritchard, Wiswall, Taylor, Coward, Lightburn Abel, Wass, Bisbrown, Humphreys, Hankinson, Lake (law clerk) Marshall (secretary.) The business of the meeting was to elect a chairman for the ensuing year, and the sub- ject was discussed in private for half an hour. When the reporters were called into the room, Mr. Pritchard proposed that the best thanks of the Board be tendered to Mr. Grice for his good offices in the chair during the past year. Although it had not. been an eventful year, Mr. Once had neverthe- less discharged his duties with credit to himself and at the same time he had sustained the dignity lof the chair. Mr. Grice had devoted considerable 1 time to the duties of his position; he thought it had been his invariable practice to attend at the offices every day, and he had kept himself in touch with all the business of the Board a most essential thing in a chair- man.—Mr. Lightburn seconded the motion, remarking that Mr.Grice had been a most genial chairman and if he had erred at all it had been on the side of kindness.—Mr. Bisbrown wished to add his tribute as the yourgest mem- ber of the Board.—Mr. Grice had been unfailing in his courtesy and geniality and he had held the balance evenly, and that he held to be the one important qualifi- cation in a chairman.—The motion was carried by accla- mation, (aid in reply,Mr. Grice said his feelings combined somewhat of pleasure and regret. It pleased him to hear the expression of satisfaction given by them in re- ference to his occupancy of the chair. At the same time he regretted that the time had passed, for it had been a great pleasure to him to work with them,and also to feel that he had the c,onfiderrie and support of every member of the, Board, and he thanked them for it. If he had fallen short of anything during the past twelve months in conducting the business it had not been for want of intention or effort on his part. He could take credit for having attended nearly all Committee meetin,,es during I the year and he had been in touch with the work of every committee and he sincerely hoped that as time went on neither the menabers of the Board nor himself nor the ratepayers would ever have occasion to regret that he was chairman of the Board. (Applause.) Mr. (irice then proposed that Mr. Frank Wiswall be elected chairman for the ensuing year, to whom he referred in terms of eulogy.—Mr. Hankinson seconded, and said Mr. Wiswall would make a very good chairman. His genial kindness, mature judgment, and firmness of character, and the straightforward way in which he had conducted everything he had had in hand en that Board, pointed him out as a gentleman whom they could all support. He had,moreover. been of very great service to the ratepayers on the Board.—Mr.Taylor sup- ported the nomination, and the motion was carried un- animously. Mr. Wiswall then took the chair vacated by Mr. Grice, amid applause, and in thanking the mem- bers for the honour they had conferred upon him, said they had not only paid a compliment to himself, but to the company he represented. Although he was not elected by the ratepayers, he did not think he need tell them that he should do all he could for the interests of the town as though he were a representative of the rate- payers, and they might rest assured that he should do all he could to maintain the dignity of the office they had called upoa him to fulfil. (Applause.) The Board then went into committee to consider some private business.

DANGEROUS BLASTING OPERATIONS. The Clerk read a letter dated June 11th, from Mr. Sweetman, of Weston, complaining of the damage done by the Ship Canal to the property of people in Weston, through the blowing up of rock. They had sent a piece weighing nearly half a hundred weight and had made a hole in his property with it, but had made the hole up. His tenants were in fear and complained of being shaken by the shots. —Mr. Aaron mentioned that the piece of rock went through a wall 18 inches thick. He moved that the Clerk write to the Chairman of Directors, requesting ' his interference in the matter.—The Clerk said the authority had no power TO deal with the matter under the Public Health Act, but they might have under com- mon law. Beveral members said it was a questien between the property owners and the Ship Canal Company.—Mr. Aaron's motion was lost by a large majority.

div.p: TUB WATER SUPPLY OF STOCKTON WRATH.

In regard to the water of Stockton Death Mr. Ross, of the water department of Warrington Corporation, replied that the Corporation was quite able and willing to provide a supply of water, sufficient for the domestic use of inhabitants within the Corporation limits, Stockton Beath included, and no failure in that respect was likely to talc( place, but they would not guarantee, as desired, any greater pressure outside the limits of the borough than that afforded by the pipe communicating with the reservoir from which the supply was taken.—The Clerk gain he had also received a letter from Mr. Robert Davies who said be had seen the Chairman of the Waterworks and Mr. Ross the secretary, and Mr. Ross seemed to think that there would be a supply of water for the use of such of them as lived south of the Bridge- water Canal about as good (or nearly as good) as they were having now, and, if so, although it was not contin- uous, or, at as good a pressure as they could wish, they would he, he thought,willing to wait and see how things went on.—The subject then dropded.

div.head: BEFORE THE NIA,GISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE NIA,GISTRATES.

MAGISTERIAL UNPCNCTUILITY. At the Warrington Borough Police Court at the time for commencing the business on Tuesday morning, ten o'clock, there was no magistrate present except Mr. Garnett. He waited 25 minutes, when, being joined by no other magistrate, be proceeded with a case which could be dealt with toy one justice, and while it was being heard Alderman Sutton entered, at half-past ten. TRANSFER OF LICENSES. At the borough magistrates' court on Monday, the license of Ellen Butterworth, of the Central Hotel, Horsemarket-street, was transferred to Joseph Woodin, formerly of the Leigh Arms, Mersey-street. that of the executors of the late Edward Ross, for the refreshment room at the Central Station, was, on the application of Mr. Percy Davies, solicitor, transferred to David Mel- drum, general manager, on the Cheshire Lines Com- mittee. Licenses were also transferred from William Warburton, Little Horse Shoe, to George Edwin Turley, formerly of the Norton Arms Hotel, Halton. A/Teem-BR CHARGE OF CRIMINAL ASSAULT ON A CHILD. At the Warrington borough police court on Thursday, Luke Cranke, aged 74, a boiler keeper at White Cross Wire Works, and living in Factory Yard, was charged with committing, on the 11th inst., a criminal assault on Lucy Brown, aged 12 years, daughter of John Brown, Railway Square. Inspector Uphill, agent for the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, appeased for the prosecution and applied for a remand. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence. An employe at the White Cross Wire Works, deposed to witnessing the assault. Mr. Browne did not object to the remand, but said the defendant had lived in the town 50 years, and there had not been a single blemish upon his charac- ter. The prisoner was remanded till next Thursday, the magistrates offering to take bail, for his re-appearance, himself in £5O and two sureties of £25 each.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. I SATIIRDAY.—Before Mr. L. Voisey (in the chair, and ' Mr. John Geddes. Tnerr.—John Warburton and Richard Lowe were charged with stealing from the yard of Mr. Robert Heaton, on the 9th June' a stone beater, valued at 25.&1.—Mr. Heaton stated that he identified the stolen article as his property by a private mark upon it.— Detective Monaghan deposed that at 5.30 on Thursday evening he was in Mersey-st., when he saw Warburton coining along with the beater. When he saw witness he put the beater on the ground and stood before it. When asked where he got it from, he said "it belongs to a man around the corner, named Dick Lowe." After taking the prisoner to the Police Station, be (witness) went in pursuit of Lowe, and haying found him, asked him how he got the beater. Prisoner replied :" I bought it at a sale.' When charged at the Police Station with the theft, Warburton said "Lowe gave it me," and Lowe said, "I bought it."—Warbur- ton now said that he was coming along Scotland-road on Thursday, when Lowe came up to him and gave him the beater, saying it was his property.—The prisoners were sent to gaol for 14 days, with hard labour. MALICIOUS THREATS.—George Rivers was charged with having ore the 7th June used certain malicious threats towards his wife, causing her to be in fear for her life.—Mr. Rivers said that on Tuesday night her husband came home drunk, and for some trivial cause picked up a knife and threatened to kill her. She had been afraid to go near the house since the occurrence.—The defend- ant said he was sorry this had happened, but he was in drink at the time. Ile had no recollection of the offence cemplained of, and when sober he was sure no one could be kinder to his wife and children than he was.—Defend- ant was bound over to keep the peace for she months. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) and Aldermen Francomb and Harrison. CSIARGRB WITH THREATENING HIS MOTHEIL—James Sauce, tailor, Corporation Buildings, was charged with using threatening language to his mother, thereby caus- ing her to he in fear for her life. The prisoner pleaded net guilty.—Mrs. Sauce stated that prisoner came home to his dinner, and after eating it demanded sd. from her to pay his railway fare to Earlestown, and because she refused to give him it threatened her. She ran out of the house, and on her return found all the pots, cups, and saucers broken, and the fragments strewed in all directions. Ile had threatened to do 15 years for her, and about 3 months ago struck her with a pair of tongs.—lt appeared, however, that on the occasion in question, the defendant had used no worse language than that if she got cross he could get cross. —The complainant had been granted a warrant against her husband on the charge of threatening to kill her. The complainant was ordered to pay the costs of the warrant, 55., and the defendant was dismissed. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.-L John Bradbury and John Mullin, in Pitt-st., on the 2nd inst., were fined, Brad- bury Ss. and Mullin ss. and costs.—Edward Hansbury, in Bridge-st., on Sunday afternoon 5.3., and James Griffin, in Edelsten's-yard, on the afternoon, inst., ss. and costs.—Margaret Oakes and Mary Ann Fudge,in Dial-st., on the 6th inst.,Oakes 53. and Fudge ss.and costs.—Mary Ann Craven, on the 7th of June, in Winwick-road, 55. Ellen Roberts, in Edelsten's-yard, on the Bth of June, 55. and costs.—Samuel Stringer, in the Market-Place,on Saturday night, ss. and costs. FIGHTING.—Wm.Kay,John Riordan, and Wm. Dutton, , for fighting in Mersey-st., on the 6th inst., were bound 1 over to keep the peace. STRRET OBSTRUCTION.—Wm. and David Plinston, brokers, Back Howard-st. , for allowing a horse amd cart to stand in Bewsey-st., longer than necessary,were fused 24. 6d. each. CARD PLATING a: Boys.—Ernest Grayson, 43 Nichol- son-st., Walter Ellis, 57 Guardian-st., John Henry Barnett, 19 Howard-st., John Wm. Lea, 6 Brierley-st., Win. Bradford, 25, Howard-at., and Ernest Jones, 41 Wakefield-St., boys, were charged with playing with cards for menay, and fined 2s. 6d. each. CRURLTY TO AN Ass.—John William Barrow, hawker, Mill-st., and William Burke, a lad, son of Mary, 31 Gee-st, were charged with cruelly treating an ass on thQ 2nd inst.—P.C. Gough said that about 9.40 a.m. on thel day in question he saw the defendants in charge of a donkey and cart in Lythgoes-lane. Barrow was run- ning alongside of it and lashing it with the reins. Burke was beating it about the hind parts with a stick. They abused the animal so much that the donkey kicked the front part of the cart in, and got its hind legs over the shafts.—lnspector Dowty said he had examined the ass and it was in a state that it could only have been in through being severely beaten.—The defendants were discharged with a caution. • TUESDAIL—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman), and Mr. R. Garnett. DRUNK.—John McCabe in Marsh House-lane, on Monday afternoon, dismissed with a caution. A DRUNKEN MOTHER-SEATER.—Joseph Ward, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bank-street on Monday night, and with assaulting and heating, on the 11th inst., Hannah Hodgson, his mother.—D.S. Monaghan and Mrs. Hodgson proved the charges, the woman stating that she followed him up the street,and he ordered her back, but she would not go, and he then assaulted her. He would not work and tormented her, giving her only 2s. 6d. in a month.—Alderman. Sutton (to the prisoner) : A month's hard labour. You will have some work then.

div.p: WEDNESDAY.—Before Councillor James Fairclough. THEFT AT MACCLESFIRLD.—J4Iua Harrison and Edward Ingham,whe were wanted on a charge of stealing a pair of boots at Macclesfield,were handed over to the authori- ties of that place. UNSEEMLY Muttony:in.—Annie Daley and Elizabeth Ellen Fleming who had made 35 and 38 appearances, respectively, were charged with objectionable behaviour in Scotland-road, the plevious night. They were each sent to prison for 14 days' hard labour. TIIUMDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley (chairman), Major Pickmere, and Councillor James Fairclough. AN ABSENTEE MILITIAMIN.—JOhn McDonough was charged with being an absentee from the training of the militia in 1890 and 1891. 40s. and costs. SCHOOL CASES.—The following persons were prosecuted by Mr. Cr. Riley for not sending their children regularly to school :—George Appleby 2s. 6d. ; Thomas Chrimes 55. ; John McLoughlin 10s. ; James Painter 55.; Char- lotte Plunkett 2s. 6d.; Thomas Robinson 55.; Mary Towey ss. ; Joseph Williams ss. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), and Alderman Wright. ABSENT FROM MILITIA TRAINING.—JOIIII Coyne, for being absent from the annual training of the 3rd South Lancashire militia, was fined 40s. and costs. MILITARY UNSERTERS.—Joseph Forbes, charged with being a deserter since May 7th from H.M. Cheshire Regi- ment stationed at Sheffield, and Patrick O'Mare charged with deserting on the 11th inst., from H.M. Royal Irish regiment, stationed at Curragh, were remanded to Strangeways gaol to await escorts. CHARGES OF ASSAULT AND THREATENING.,--POLITICS Amorea WOMEN.—flenry Delooze, of Winwick-St., was charged with assaulting, on the 7th inst. Eliza. Roberts, of 4 Edelsten's Yard. Mr. Forshaw appeared for the prosecution. The prosecutrix, a girl aged 13, said the defendant ran into her mother's house after her following ker upstairs, and struck her in the breast and eye.—The defendant was fined 10s. and costs. Emma Hayes, 90, Lythgoes-lane and Mary Jane Hayes, 65, Lythgoes-lane. summoned each other for assault and Alice Morris, 73, Lythgoes-lane, was charged with threatening Emma Hayes, on the 11th inst. The evid- euce disclosed the use of some most horrible languageon the part of the first two defendants, and that the quarrel had commenced through an argument about politics.— Emma Hayes was bound over in the sum of £lO to keep the peace for 6 months, and the other cases were dis- , missed.—Alice Higham, wife of Daniel Higham, 8, Ernest-street, and Sarah Ann Skelton, 9, Selby-street, were charged with threatening each other.—Skelton was dismissed, and Higham bound over in £5 to keep the peace, and mulcted in costs.

WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Major Pickmere (chairman), and Mr. R. Armitage. DM:Mg.—Annie Weaton, drunk at Sankey Bridges, ss. and costs.—Martin Bury, at Sankey Bridges on the 17th inst., ss. and costs. A LAmrLisss Crcrx.—Frederick Binks, was charged with riding a bicycle on the night of the 9th inst., at Sankey Bridges, without having a lighted lamp. To pay costa. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Wm. Platt, at Poulton, on the 6th inst., 10s. and costs. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A HORSE—James Dason drunk in charge of a horse and lurry, on the 16th of May, at Poulton, 103. and costs. RIDING ON THE FOOTPATH.—James Pemberton, for riding a bicycle A n the footpath at Southworth on the 6th inst., was fined is. and costs. ILL-TREATING LIORSES.—John Smith was charged by Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., with causing a mare to be worked while in an unfit state on the sth inst, and Jas. Worsley was charged with working the animal. The horse was being driven with a waggonette filled with passengers while suffering from a large wound on the shoulder, under the collar. Smith 20s. land costs, and Worsley 55. and costs.—Geo. Colville, of Rixton, was charged with ill-treating a horse there on the 31st of May. Mr. Jenkins appeared for the prosecu- tion.—John Challon, employed by Mr. Edward Lunt, ' carting contractor, Church-st., Warring;ton,deposed that on the 24th March by the instructions of Mr. Lunt, he delivered the mare to the aefendant in good working condition. It was brought back with its bones almost through the skin through being over worked and underfed —Mr. Lunt said the defendant hired the horse from him I at 15s. a week. On the 31st May he found the mare in the defendant's stables with only chopped straw and hay to I eat, and she was nothing but a ruck of bones. He com- plained to the defendant, and brought the animal back two days after. The mare was so weak that it would take her three months to recover—The defendant said he could count every rib the mare had when she came to i I his place. He used her for ploughing, as she was not in a fit state to go on the road.—Mr. Lunt : Well, she was on the road, before you got her.—ln reply to the I Bench, witness said he went to the defendant's, becauae he was told that if he didn't he would have to take a " knackering cart" to fetch her.—Samuel Lunt said the mare when she came back was a complete skeleton.— James Hewitt, veterinary surgeon, corroborated, and said the mare had been kept short of food.—lnspector Dowty said that he found the mare staggering with weakness in the defendant's stable, hidebound, and wasted, on the 2nd of June. He had seen it previous to going there in good working condition. He considered the defendant had overworked and underfed it. If it were his mare he would send it to the knacker's yard.— The defendant denied the charge, and called Luke Flannaglian, who said it had been brought in poor con- dition, and the defendant fed it well on Indian corn, oats and "chops." He told his master he would hose to send for the horse doctor. The day after coming the mare could scarcely walk. Pressed as to why he worked the horse in such a condition he could only answer : "They say she was in good condition when she came."—Thomas Crane corroborated .—The defendant was fined 20s. and

costs. BREACHES OF THE WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT.—James Williams, manure manufacturer, of Cuerdley, was charged with having in his possession on the 9th of June three weighing machines unjust, also with having them unstamped. Inspector Spencer proved the case, and debosed that the machines were platform machines for weighing bags of manure. When 71bs weight was I placed on the platform they were tlb. against the pur- chaser, when 14lb. was on they were Alb. against the purchaser, and so on. The machines were also un- stamped. The defendant was fined 10s. and costs in each case. VAGRANCY.—Alexander Unswo rth, of Hollins Gran, for this offence at Martinscroft on the 14th inst., was sent to jail for seven days' hard labour.

div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr, Jam's Reynolds and Major
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr, Jam's Reynolds and Major
Haztehurst.

TEMPORARY AIITHORITY.—Thomas Davies was granted permission to sell at the Mersey Vaults, Mersey-street, under the license lately held by Alfred Bailey. DRllNK.—Joseph Clayton, Mary Foy, and Edith Evans were each fined for drunkenness. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—EIiVII/CIII Oliver and Margaret Connolley, were each ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for six months for fighting in Mersey-street on the 7tit June. GAMBLERS.—Thomas Robinson, Thos. Flannigan, John Flannigan, and Joseph Bushell, youths, were convicted of gaming with cards on the Fair Ground on Sunday the 29th May, and a fine of 103., including costs, was im- posed upon each defeadant.—For gaming by pitch and , toss in Collier-st., Thomas Worrall, Herbert Leach, and Frederick Albinson were discharged with a caution. ASSAULTS.—Mary Ann Probin summoned Mary Ann Harold for an assault, and there was a cross-summons charging Probin with assaulting Harold. The Bench bound both over to keep the peace for six months.—John Gratton was summoned for assaulting Mary Ann Probin and he also was bound over.—Rebecca Bazley was bound over for assaulting Elizabeth Inglesfield, and the latter was discharged on a similar charge made by Bazley. SCHOOL BOARD Casss.- Nine parents were summoned for not sending their children regularly to school,and the usual fine of 6d. and costs 4s. 61. was imposei. SLEEPING OllT.—George Taylor and William Price were charged with sleeping on the premises of Farmer Finch at Halton, and Charles N. Brown with committing a similar offence on the premises of Reuben Peacock, Greenway-road.—A sentence of seven days' hard labour was passed on each prisoner. RESISTING THE POLlCE.—Richard Whitelock, a young man was charged with resisting P.S. Gosling whilst in the execution ot Ids duty in Nelson-st., on the Bth June. Evidence was given showing that the defendant at- tempted to rescue a prisoner whom the officer had in custody.—A fine of ss. and costs was inflicted.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. J. Ifirchall and Mr. E. Mather. DRUNKENNESS.—John Lea, no fixed abode, and John Foster, Rainhill, were each fined for drunkenness. John Cusick, of Midwood-st., was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and als3. with assaulting P.C. Almond. On Saturday night the cen,table took the prisoner into custody on the first charge, and on the way to the Police Station he threw himself to the ground and severely kicked the Constable about the legs. He was very violent.—For being drunk a fine of 2s. 61 and costs was imposed and for the assault 55. and costa.° Ax UNPROVOKED ASSAULT.—lsabella Kearneg, Nelson- st.,a young married woman was charged with committ- ing an aggravated assault on a neighbour named Bridget Murphy. It was alleged that between mine and ten o'clock on the night of the 9th inst., the prisoner met the prosecutrlx in the street, and without any pro- vocation took off one of her hoots and struck the prose- cutrix about the head and arms.—Dr. Hutchinson said the woman had a wound 3.-I,ins. tom; on the back of the head.—The prisoner was fined 105. and costs and ordered to also pay 103. 61 doctor's fee, or a month's imprison- ment. —The prisoner said she would go to gaol.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 18. 1892/
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 18. 1892/
CRICKET.

Secretaries of Cricket Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than iana o'clock on Wednesday morning.

WESTON V. WINNINGTON " A."—Played at Winning- ton, on Saturday, and resulted in a draw. Total, Weston, 75 ; Winnington, 46. LATCHFORD ST. MARY'S V. EMMANUEL CHURCH CHOIR. —Played oa the ground of the former on Saturday. 'core : Emmanuel Church, 23 ; Latchford, 52. ST. PETER'S CHOTR (WARRINGTON) T. WHITE STAR. —This match was played on the ground of the former, and resulted in a win for the home team by 48 runs. Score :—St. Peter's, 73; White Star, 25. ST. PAUL'S CHOIR (WARRINGTON) V, TRINITY CHOIR. —This match was played on the ground of the latter, and resulted in a win for the former, the score being— St. Paul's Choir, 78 runs ; Trinity Choir, 39 runs. ST. PAUL'S CHOIR C. C. V. TRINITY CHOIR CC.— This match was played on the ground of the latter, and resulted in a win for the former. The score was St. Paul's Choir C.C. 78 ;Trinity choir C.C. 39. ORFORD CRESCENT V. PADGATIA 2ND C.C.—This match was played on the ground of the latter club, the ground being in a wet condition and resulted in a win for the Crescent by six runs. The Crescent played a very weak team having 4 subs., the only prominent players of the teams being W. Ball, who made 10 runs and took 5 wickets for 8 runs. Score :—Orford Crescent 25 ; Pad- gate second, 19. WARRINGTON Y. SEFTON.—This match was played at Sefton Park, on Saturday, The heavy rain of Friday had not affected the wicked to any great extent, but an hour before the advertised time to start rain came down in torrents, and it was 3.45 before Messrs. Smith and J. J. Crosfield took their place at the wickets, to the bowling of F. Jones and Oakley. Smith soon got to work, and after putting 15 together. he was splendidly taken at mid off by Champion from a hard drive. Clarke joined Crosield, but alter making a single played tamely at one from Oakley, and two wickets were down for 20. Dis- aster did not stay here, for the first ball Bell received proved too much for him. Voisey made a gallant effort to stay the rot" which had set in, but he had only totalled nine when Jones bowled him with an extra last one. J.. 1. Cies-field left at the same total-29—having been at the wickets 35 minutes for four. At 32 Dutton fell a victim to Ratcliffe's smarteess behind the wickets. It was left to Clark and R. Brown to retrieve the lost position for Warrington, and a useful stand was made. At 46 Chautpion took the ball from Jones, and with the addition of nine runs Clark was caught at mid off for an invaluable 20. Brown continued to bat steadily, and in conjunction with Pedmore another slight stand was made, having helped to raise the total from 55 to 66, when he was got in two minds, and of course, paid the penalty, whilst at 75 Podmoro ran out to drive Champion. Crompton failed to survive the second ball ke received, and the innings closed for 75, Monks taking I out his bat for 5. The collapse of Warrington in the early portion of the innings was, indeed, remarkable, as the wicket certainly favoured the batsman. Messrs. C. L. Jonbi and U. A. Pope first represented Sefton, and the first-named soon got to work, and got Smith's expresses twice to the boundary in the first two overs. Runs were piled on at a rapid pace, Jones scoring much the faster so at 46 Bell took the oval from his captain, whilst the latter crossed over to Smith's end. The change worked,l for at 51 Jones was bowled for 30. His innings were marred by several chances, one being a ridiculously easy one when the score was at 21. Stubbs joined Roper,and a valuable stand was made. Changes were frequently made, but to no purpose, and the visitors' total was soon passed At 71 Crosfield brought off a fine catch, which dismissed Roper. Little interest was taken in the cricket which followed, but the fielding of Podmore is worthy of mention. At the closa of the day's sport Sefton were in a majority of 52 runs, and still had four wickets to fall. Score and bowling analysis : WARRINGTON. div.head: KNUTSFORD DIVISION.
div.p: THE KNUTSFORD DIVISION.

fIIE CANDIDATURE OF MR. A. W. LATHAM . On Thursday evening a meeting in support of Mr. Latham, the Liberal candidate for the Knutsford division, was held in a field near Mr. J. Wiuser's house at Grappenhall. The meeting was timed to begin at seven o'clock, but owing to a misunder- standing as to the time, Mri.nLiattnliaampp gose who had intended to ewa raasn cael °lnt Iti the f -ma ne meantime el aat e plew ouit t ti be present at the meeting had left. There was, not- witnstanding, a satisfactory attendance, chiefly of workingmen. There was present in the village one of the Home Rule Union vans from which literature was distributed. The chair was taken by Mr. W. Davidson who remarked that he was well ac- quainted with the candidate's father, as they laboured many years together for the benefit of agricultural dis- tricts. They assisted in carrying on, as long as they could, the Farmers Alliance, and he believed they had thereby something to do with getting the Agricultural Holdings Act pasted,but the Act hadeike all Acts passed by the Tories, been spoiled by the insertion of a clause which permitted landlords to contract out of the Act. (Rear, near, and applause.) Mr. Latnain, who was well received, said that if they returned him as their member lie should be very happy to come amongst them whenever they wanted him. He came before them as a Liberal, and he asked them to vote for bins as a Liberal. He would support Liberal measures and bo a staunch follower of Mr. Gladstone. (Rear, hear.) Nediat was the real difference between Liberals and Conservatives ? He thought it was this— that the Liberals were willing to trust the people, while the Conservatives would have none of it. (Hear, hear.) The present 6ro !eminent, while they had been in power, had passed some measures of a Liberal character, but it they looked carefully they would find in them the cloven hoof of Conservatism. (Rear, hear.) The Local Government Act which created County Councils provided for the appointment of Alder- men who were not elected by the people. Had that measure been a thoroughly Liberale'one they should not have had any such nonsense as Aldermen, and the con- trol ex Use joaiao would. also have laaeu put into the hands of the people. (Hear hear.) The Small Holdings Bill also showed the cloven hoot .f Conservatism, because the Government had ("teamed tc put in compulsory clauses. Then there was the Assisted Education Act by which the government made grants of public money in aid of education but left it in the hands of the parson and the squire. What chance had a working-man to look alter the education of his children unlese he had some voice in the management of the whole thing? The schools Should, by means of Parish Councils, pe put haw the hands of the people, and they would be etble to say whether or not they would allow meetings to be held in them. At present the clergyman of that stieteCould prevent either Liberals or Conservatives, i he liked, from meeting in the schools. It they returned the Liberals to power at that election they would be given the management of their own affairs through their parish councils. They must have control of their allot- ments, their schools and education, their parish or village hails, and above all they inuet have control of the licens- ing, so that they could say how many public-houses they would have withid.their boundaries. He had been told by many workii gown that what they desired above all things was a Mt of land, bat, in °eller to get that, they must be placed in a position to ge to the landlort and tell him that they wanted a certain piece of land for allotments, and that the landlord should not be able to refuse on being paid the market price for the land. It was also necessary that the I allotment holder should have the same protection as the farmer, and compensation for all his improvements. (Applause.) eels J. H. Fairfax, (secretary of the Allotments and Small Holding's Association) moved that Mr. Latham was a fit and proper person to represent the constitu- ency, and pledging the meeting to use all legitimate , ' means to secure his return. Captain Rogers seconded the proposition. Questions having been invieed, Mr. Jenkins asked what were the views of the candidate oa the eight hours ' question, especially in view of Mr. Gladstone's position. it would be useless giving workinguien allotments un- less they had time to cultivate them, (Hear, hear.) ' Mr. Latham said he was in favour of an eight hours day for miners, but he could not pledge himself to sup- port a universal eight hours Bill. His position was that of trade option. If a large majority of the workmen of any trade were in favour of an eight hours Bill he would vote for it. In answer to other questions, Mr. Latham said he did not think the subject of the disestablishment and diseudowment of the church would be dealt with in the next Parliament, although he was in favour of it. He was also in favour of a large extension of the suff- rage, though not quite to the full extent of manhood suffrage. A vote of thanks to the Chairman, moved by Mr. J. Price, concluded the meeting. MEETING AT STOCKTON HEATH. Mr. Latham afterwards proceeded to Stockton Heath, e. well-attended meeting was held in the open space near the Police Station. --- Captain Rogers, who presided, referred to the great political services of the canaidate's father, and added that he had no doubt their candidate would be an equally good supporter of Radical principles. Mr. Lathom, who was again well reeeived, said he had no hesitation in saying that he was strongly in favour of Home Rule for Ireland. He believed that if they had Home Rule for Ireland there woald be more pros- perity in that country. This would prevent the great influx of Irishmen into England by giving them employment at home. That was a matter of great importance to English agricultural labourers. (Hear, hear.) The Government which was now in power had never done anything for the farmer or agricultural labourer, or what they had done had been forced on them by the Liberals and had been spoiled by the Conservative majority. (Hear, hear.) He quoted as an instance the Education Act, by which public money was given to the Church schools, which were run by the parson, who did what he liked with the money. Rethought it wae a crying scandal that such a thing should be in this country ; for, where even the smallest contribution was made from public funds, there should be public represensativee to control the spending of it. (Hear, hear.) He also alluded to the necessity for the sanitary arrangements of rural districts being placed under the control of popularly elected bodies ; he not only advocated Home Rule for Ireland but also Home Rule for themselves as well. (Applause.) Mr. A. H. Crosfield, in moving a resolution similar to that passed at the other meeting, said Mr. Latham asked for their support because he was in favour of the reforms included in the Newcastle programme, and because he advocated Home Rule. They had heard it said in a great many quarters lately that they were attempting to throw Home Rule into the background. That was a rather bold assertion. Anyone who had read the papers would think that Home Rule had had a fair share of their attention during the last six years. (Hear, hear.) It was not their interest to put Home Rule in the background. They were committed to it and they were glad they were committed to it, and they knew that the chief foundation to the opposition to Home Rule was after all, prejudice and misconception, and, he might say, ignorance, and the more they drove the realities of the case into the minds of the electorate the more they should dissipate that which was the foundation of their opponents' case. (Rear, hear.) It was quite true that the Liberals, having made up their minds as to the only sensible solution of the Irish question, were turning their attention to other things. There were constantly rising up in their great cem- munity questions that forced themselves to the front, and that could not be shelved—questions that were the result of their enormovs increase in population, and the increasing complexity of their social relations, and of their increasing wealth, and commerce. It was one of the evils of the unsettlement of the Irish question that their representatives in Parliament had their attention absorbed, by that question to the exclusion of those things that should properly come within the sphere of their political interests and activity. (Hear, bear.) A great deal was going to be said abont .Ingrer. At the start the cry of separation was the one in which their opponents put their faith, but now it was that of Ulster. Be believed, however, that the electors of this country would soon tee that " Ulstoria" was very much like hysteria, and that there was as little in it as there was in the cry, of separation. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. Benjamin seconded the resolution, which was carried, and the meeting concluded with votes of thanks

TERRIBLE A ItTILLERY ACCIDENT. TWO SOLDIERS BLOWN TO PIECES. MAGDEBURG, Tull USDAY. —As some soldiers were unloading an ammunition waggon containing shells at the barracks ot the Foot Artillery to-day one of the shells exploded with terrible effect. The heads of two sergeants and the arms and legs of another were blown off, while a sergeant-major received severe injury.

div.head: ORIENTAL-BANK FAILURE.
div.p: THE ORIENTAL-BANK FAILURE.

A meeting of the shareholders of the Oriental Bank, which recently suspended Dayment,was held at Cannonst., Hotel, on Thursday, to consider the question as to whether the Bank should go into voluntary liquidation, so as to avoid the costly and cumbrous process of com- pulsory liquidation. The .meeting ultimately resolved on voluntary liquidation, and agreed to appoint Mr. T. Welton the official liquidator.

div.head: BOWLS.
div.p: BOWLS.

PUKING, ON'S (ST. HELENS) PLATE Wo nits v. DOWNALL GREEN.—The above game was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday, being the first off-match for the Plate Works. The weather was somewhat showery, but this was rather in favour of the visitors, and they un- doubtedly utilised this advantage to the full, as after a most exciting game they managed to win by 14 points. This is all the more creditable seeing that Downall Green are a very strong team' and on their own turf are regarded•as unconquerable. Score :—Plate Works, 262 ; Downall Green, 248. After the game the teams ad- journed to the Blue Bell Inn, where a substantial tea was partaken of, the catering being in Mr. and Mrs. Neill's best style. At the after proceedings Mr. Aspinall pre- sided, and Mr. J. Preston took the vice-chair.

div.head: MURDER OF A-SWEETHEART.
div.p: MURDER OF A-SWEETHEART.

At the Old Hill Police Court, on Wednesday, Harry Pugh, 29, miner, was committed for trial on the charge of wilfully murdering his sweetheart, Ann Maria Gill, 28, on the 25th May, by drowning her in a reservoir at Cradley Heath. After committing the, deed the pri- soner attempted suicide.

div.head: COLLAPSE OF A BRIDUE.
div.p: COLLAPSE OF A BRIDUE.

LOSS OF THIRTY LIVES. New Youx, WEDNESDCf.—A telegram received here announces that a bridge which was being constructed over the Licking River, in Kentucky, connecting the towns of Covington and Newport, and was approaching completion, suddenly collapsed to-day. All the men employed at the time on the structure, numbering, it is said, a dozen, were killed. Another' despatch states that it was the woodwork of the bridge which fell, and that thirty perished, and that up to the present sixteen bodies have been recovered. ON OATH'. :Mr. Norman Tate. div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The mOnthly raeelitig of this Board was held at the Town Hall, Widnes, on Tuesday afternoon. In the absence of the Chairman Mr: Hayes presided, and there were also present Messrs. tCook, Wright, Brown, Houghton, Neil, Owens, Beech. Taylor, Sadler; Craik (deputy clerk), and other officers.

div.head: GAS AND -MATER :COMMITTER.
div.p: GAS AND -MATER :COMMITTER.

This Committee recommended that the following ten- ders for coal be accepted :—The Abram Coal Company, 5,000 tons Arley Slack, at 7s. per ton; Simpson, Davies, and Sons, 5,000 tons at 7s. per ton ; W. and J. Richard- son, 3,000 tons gas nuts at 75.10 d. per ton: The water' engineer reported that the mean rainfall for the month had been 3,225 inches. The illuminating power, of the gas during the month had averaged 1795 candles. The profit and loss account for the year ending March 1892, showed as follows :—Gas account, profit, J 22,848 Os. 4d. ; water (excluding expenditure on Netherley extension account), £B4O 12s. 2d. —Mr. Brown, in moving the confirmation of the mingtes, said there had been an increased consumption of gas, with perhaps quite as much economy in work- ing, and the profits were, he thought, satisfactory. The water accounts did not turn out quite so well as the gas. The profit was £B4O, but that did not include the ex- penditure they were under at Netherley. Reckoning that expenditure they had a loss of £72o.—Mr. Taylor seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Sadler asked if anything had been done in regard to adopting penny- in-the-slot gas meters. They were working very satis- factorily in other towns, and as many as 4,000 were fixed in Liverpool.—Mr. Brown said that as the meters seemed to be fairly workable and successful the Committee would begin to think seriously about adopting them.— The minutes were then adopted.

div.head: inartwAy COMMITTER.
div.p: inartwAy COMMITTER.

The minutes of this committee stated that, with regard to the level crossing, Tanhouse-lane, the Clerk reported that 'as instructed at the last meeting he had written to the.M.S. and L. RailWay,Co. with reference to the discontinuance of the wicket gates, and he sub- mitted and read the Co.'s reply, stating that "the wicket gates had been dispensed with at the instance of the Board of Trade, whose inspecting officer had called their_attention to the desirability of such proceeding in thelnterest of public safety." -It -wee recommended that the Chairman and Mr. Taylor bn appointed to pur- chase a horse for the department. Plans for the following had been submitted and approved :—One house, Salis- bury-st., for John Philips two houses Frederick-st., for John Forshaw.—On the motion of Mr. Sadler the minutes were passed.

THP HEALTH COMMITTEE. This Committee reported that since the last meetint two patients had been admitted to the Accident hospital and two to the Infectious Diseases hospital. The Medical officer reported that " the township has been very free from zymotic diseases during the month. I have visited both hospitals several times during the month, and found everything satisfactory. , It will be a great pleasure to the gentlemen of the Board, as well as tu the ratepayersin general, to hear, that there has been no escape of IHMIOGS vapours during the month. It shows that greater vigilance is observed now than for- merly by the managers of the variouS works, and in laying the waste in order to prevent the escape of noxious gases. I have not heard of any complaint from any part isf the town, and it is to be hoped that this satisfactory state of things will long continue." The Committee reported that "The M.. 0. H. having drawn the attention of the Committee to the condition of certain dwellinghouses situate and being Nos. 34 to 88 inclusive, Cromwell-street, which he described as unfit for human habitation, the Committee proceeded to inspect the same and resolved that unless the property be forthwith put into a proper sanitary state, the necessary steps be taken to have the same declared unfit for human habitation, and also resolved that the attention of the Highway Committee be drawn to the state of the several streets and passages in the neighbourhood of the above property, and ,to the urgent necessity for causing such streets and passages Au) be properly and effid- ently made, paved, and sewered." It was recom- mended that the • teader of Mr. G. Steinart, £39 10s., for glazing market roof be accepted.— Mr. Wright moved the confirmation of these minutes, and said the Owners' and Occupiers' Association had been kind enough to make a presentation to the charity fund of eleven guineas, and he moved that a vote of thanks be given to the Association for their kind act. (Hear, hear.) He added that the attention e“he Com- mittee had been called to the condition of Nelson-st., Cromwell-st., and other streets in that locality, the back yards and passages there being in a very bad con- ditiou.—Mr. Cook, in seconding the confirmation of the minutes, said he could bear testimony to the very in- sanitary condition in which they had found that part of thetown. It must be very injurious to the inhabit- ants as well as to the general health of the town.—Mr. Beech said these streets had been left in the condition they were in simply because they belonged to a mem- ber of ths Board.—Mr. Sadler asked to whom the in- sanitary street belonged.—Mr. Wright said he was told the property belonged to the Chairman of the Fieance Committee.—Mr. Taylor said he did not know to whom they belonged, but they were a disgrace.—The minutes CORlMitnurawere then adoptesi. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

In this Committee's minutes it was stated as follows : —Bowers Brook : better, May 24th, from the United Alkali, Co., Limited, enclosing copy of a letter received by them from the L. and N.-W. Railway Co.' in which it was stated that the matter of the Brook had again been brought befere the Directors of the Railway Co., for consideration, and they saw no reason to alter their previous decision, on the subject, read. The Clerk stated the position of.the matter, and referred to the pre- vious letters from the United Alkali Co. ,Limited, and to to the understanding come to in February last, whereby the Railway Co. were to enlarge the culverts on their property, and the United Alkali Co. to undertake to do the remainder of the work and to keep the brook free from obstruction in the future. He also reported the result of an interview he had had with the United Alkali Co., at which it had been suggested that he should see Mr. Mason, Solicitor to the Railway Co., with a view to ascertaining the reason for the change in the attitude of the Railway Co. Resolved that the Clerk ,be authorised to wait upon Mr. Mason as suggested.—Pro- menade Wall : Referring to the resolution of this Com- mittee passed at the last meeting, the Clerk submitted and read letter, 28th May, from the Secretary to the Manchester Ship Canal Co., enclosing cheque for £l5O, which the Company were prepared tq contribute to- wards the cost of repairs to the wall, and he was in- structed to • sign and forward to the Company the formal receipt for the amount, also submitted. --Vehicu- ler Bridge : The Clerk reported that he and the Sur- veyor, together with Mr. Alderman Snape, and Mr. H. Wade-Deacon, C,C., had attended the first meeting of the Sub-Committees of the Lancashire and Cheshire County Councils, held at the County Session House, Islington, Liverpool, on the 25th tilt, when the matter was partially considered and the meeting adjourned. Recommended that the Clerk arrange a meeting between this Committee and a Committee of the Runcorn Im- provemeut Conimissioners for the purpose of further discussing the question and deciding upon the line of action to be taken before the Joint Committee.—Mr. Beech moved, and Mr. Wright seconded the adoption of the minutes, which was agreed to: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION. The Technical Instruction Committee recommended that Mr. W. Harrison, 8.A., be paid £2O instead of £l2 for hie services as teacher of the mathematics and short- hand classes during the past session. It was also recom- mended that £2O be paid to Mr. S. Hoyle, secretary out of the money granted by the County Council, as salary for his services during the past session.—The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Mr. Brown. THE FAIR WAGE CLAUSES.

Mr. Sadler proposed "That the following clauses be in- serted in the Local Board's contract for works viz.:-That a contractor in carrying out this contract shall pay the rate of wages and observe the hours of labour recognised and agreed upon by Trades Unions and employers respec- tively in the district of Widnes, or such rate of wages and hours as are equivalent and approximate thereto; and the contraltor shall not transfer, assign, or underlet directly or inatrecuy, 'Ulla contract, or any part, share.. or interest therein, without the written consent of the Local Board under the hand of their clerk." He was sure that none of the members of the Board would wish that the men employed by the Board should be placed in a worse position than those of other similar authorities, and the clauses he was proposing had been adopted by the London County Council, and various Corporations in thEir immediate neighbourhood.—Mr. Beech seconded the proposal, and said that its adoption would put an end to the inferior workmanship of which they had had a great deal, and which had thrown a great amount of labour upon their surveyor, and those under him.—Mr. Brown hoped that the resolution would be of some practical value. He saw that in London the sweaters or middlemen had been dispensed with, but the masters themselves did thg sweating now, and only paid tho same prices as the sweaters did.—Mr. Sadler : Oh, we have in. objection to the masters sweating.—The resolution was the adopted without dissent.

div.head: WIFE MURDER IN LONDON.
div.p: WIFE MURDER IN LONDON.

At the Westminster Town Flail, on Wednesday, the coroner opened an inquiry into the circumstances attend ing the death of Maria Taylor, who is alleged to have been murdered by her husband, James Taylor, on the morning of Monday last.—Evidence was given to the effect that the deceased was lying on the bed with her skull fractured. A baby was lying by her side asleep and uninjured. A wooden roller covered with blood was standing against a mangle in the room.—After some further evidence the jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against James Taylor, who was commit- ted for trial on the coroner's warrant.

THE REVOLTING CHARGE AGAINST A

gITHER. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Thursday, Daniel Massey, widower, hairdresser and umbrella maker, 77, Winwick-road, was brought up on remand from Tuesday, charged with committ- ing on the 4th and sth inst., a criminal assault on his daughter, Edith Massey, aged 12i years. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk, appeared for the pro- secution and Mr. Forshaw for the defence.—Mr. Whittle said 114 bad been unable to elicit any in- formation from the child,who denied that anything of the sort with the prisoner had taken place. Mr. Whittle, however, produced ,photographs of the the prisoner's house in one of which Inspector Spinks was standing at the bedroom window in 'a sheet, the object being to show that certain ob- servations made by neighbours could be relied on. Mary Jane Hankinson, of 72, Winwick-road, opposite the prisoner's house, deposed to witnessing at midnight, on Saturday the 4th inst., from her bedroom window, through tile bedroom windevr of the prisoner's house, certain scandalous conduct on his part towards his daughter. in reply to Mr. Forshaw witness admitted that they might have been teasing each other. She could not swear to the commission of an assault. Mary Ann Foden, wife of Wm. Foden, Emma Devon, wife of John Devon, the husbands of these two women, and Mary Poole, wife of John Poole, deposed to witness- ing in the same way on Sunday night, the sth init., similar conduct by the prisoner. Dr. Starkdy Smith gave evidence, and Inspector Spike and Sergeant Cheney deposed te prisoner's arrest, and his declaring that he was innocent, and on hearing what Dr. Smith's opinion was, exclaiming " It must have been the lads." Inspector Spinks also gave evidence as to the photograph previously mentioned. The child herself was twice brought before the court ' to be sworn, but could not be induced to kiss the Testa- ment or to utter a word.—Mr. Forshaw contended that there was no evidence to prove his client's guilt, and ' the case was one of mere suppesition. The Bench committed the prisoner for trial at the Assizes, refusing to admit him to bail. The prisoner who reserved his defence, will be tried ! about the 26th ultimo

div.head: IMPENDING DISSOLUTION.
div.p: THE IMPENDING DISSOLUTION.

We (*Times") may venture to assume that, if Parlia- ment is dissolved, as is most likely, on the 28th, the borough elections may begin on Monday, July 4th, and the issue of the battle may be practically known on the 13th or 14th of that month. The new Parliament can- not meet until thirty-five days after the issue of the writs, that is, in the case supposed. not till August 4th. The Opposition have begun to raise an outcry against Mr. Balfour's calculations because the arrrangement suggested would not allow the elections to be univer- sally fixed for a Saturday. The Gladstonian leaders are of opinion that the work of the session might be concluded in time for the writs to be posted on Saturday, the 25th, but various preliminary arrangements, such as the provision of special trains, &c., are necessary in con- nection with meetings of the Privy Council,and in fixing the dates for such meetings it is thought best that a sufficient margin should be allowed to preclude the possibility of postponement at the last moment; but the most remarkable fact is that Mr. Balfour proposes now to introduce about a dozen new hills, most of them, it is true, raising little controversy, of which nothing has hitherto been heard. CABINET COUNCIL. A Cabinet Council was held at half-past eleven on Wednesday morning in Mr. Balfour's Private room at the House of CommonS, so that Ministers might be within reach of the house in case their presence was necessary. Lord Salisbury arrived early from Arlington-st. Lord Ashbourne attended, having reached London on Wednes- day morning from Dublin, and all the other Ministers were present except Lord George Hamilton all Lord Cidagan. MR. GLADSTONE'S ADDRESS. „ A special correspondent states that Mr. Gladstone's address to the electors of Midlothian, in which he will explain the general principles on which he intends to deal wall the Irish question, is expected to be issued in the course of next week. THE CHOICE OF DAY. The London Trades Council Executive on Thursday decided to communicate with Mr. Balfour,-requesting him to make the dissolution of Parliament fall on such a day as will enable the returning officers to arrange for . the elections to take place on a Saturday.

The Central News says :—The Council for the trans- action of the formalities necessarily attending the disso- lution of Parliament will be held on Tuesday the 28th Inst., and the Royal proclamation dissolving Parliament will be published in the "London Gazette ' of the same evening. By this arrangement the borough elections will take place during the week commencing Monday, 4th July, and none of them can occur on a Saturday. The first county election will take place on Tuesday, sth July.
Mrs. Parnell, mother of the late Irish leader, visited her son's grave, on Wednesday, in Glasuevin Cemetery, and placed a wreath of flowers upon it. She left for America on Thursday.
