div.p: 7Lttters to tin Obttor.
JUSTICE TO IRELAND.

Sir,—! do not see why the people of Ireland should not manage the internal affairs of their own country. The residents in the Isle of Man are allowed to cenduct their own business. They have the House of Keys which considers the wants of the people on the island, and I think the affairs of the Isle of Man are managed satis- factorily ; at least, Englishmen are always happy with the residents upon their visit to the island. Ireland is tile next island to the Isle of Man. Why should there be a difference? Can any of your readers inform me? —Yours, tzc., June 18th, 1892.
BRITISH WORKMAN.

div.head: WHITSUNTIDE GIFT .TO . NORTH COUNTRY
div.p: WHITSUNTIDE GIFT .TO . NORTH COUNTRY
INFIRMARIES.

fifir,—The masses in Lancashire, my native county, and in Yorkshire, have been very good friends to me during my two-and-twenty years' trading amongst them. I started business with a small capital but with high hopes. My most sanguine expectations have been ful- filled, and fortune has smiled on me. A natural feeling a thankfulness to the toiling millions of Lancashire itupels me to do what I can to show my gratitude to them. And having regard to the noble work done for all sections of our community by the Maachester Infir- mary, I have sent a draft for £5OO as a donation to ita funds. I have also sent similar cheques ts kindred in- stitutions in Leeds and Bradford. As my business is about to become less personal in its proprietorship, I think this a fitting time to give effect to a private inten- tion which I have long cherished .—Yours, &c., ARTHUR BROOKE. 17 and 18, St. Dunstan's-hill, Lcndon, June 4th.

div.head: PATENT-LAW REFORM ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE PATENT-LAW REFORM ASSOCIATION.

Sir,—lt will be exceedingly gratifying to your readers who wish to see long-delayed justice done to Inven- tors, to learn that a large number of gentlemen, true to the interests of poor and rich alike, have become Vice-Presidents of this Association since it was made public, on the 24th May. Leading Liberal names are coming in daily. No less than 20 Liberal Candidates have already joined the Association, to advocate justice for Inventors, through the adoption of the American Patent System. Inventors did very wisely to appeal to the Liberal party to redress their grievances. None other than Liberals will go to the root of the evil of the present system.—Yours, &c., R. p. JOHNSON,..F.R.A.S., Hon. Sec.
1, Lord-street, June 15th, 189. ALLEGED INTOLERANCE IN IRELAND.—A
GROSS MISREPRESENTATION.

Sir,—Some time ago a paragraph went the round of the papers stating that a clergyman of the Established Church, well-knewn in connection with the fisheries in Ireland, the Rev. Mr. Greene, had met with a very up-to-date specimen of Irish bigotry in the shape of a manager of an Industrial School, in Salthill, Galway, Ireland. Political capital was made out of this supposed act of intolerance and one of our local worthies wrote the " Observer " quoting from a disgusting article written in the Galway (Tory) " Express" under the heading " They would net eat "—" Protestant fish." This gentleman who signed himself " Unionist," which in this case certainly was a misnomer, stated that the Rev. Mr. Gseene sent several boxes of mackerel for the use of the boys in the industrial school ; and that the managers of the schools returned the fish without one word of explanation, simply because the fish came from a Protestant source. Then he grew eloquent as only Tory writers and speakrs know how about " The intolerance of Roman Catholics," and he used a very choice phrase to show how impartial and unprejudiced he is in things Catholics and Irish "Monastic Gorge" is distinctly an Orange gem of the first water. I answered the calumny as best I could, sending to the " Observer " a correspondence clipped from the Galway " Express," in which it appeared that the Rev. Brother who manages the school wrote a full and satisfactory explanation to the Rev. Mr. Greene thanking him for his kindness in forwarding the fish, and regretting that it could not be used in the schools. I also personally requested the editor of the " Observer " to publish this correspondence in last Saturday's issue, and lam very sorry he did not see his way to do so. I shall be very glad if you would kindly publish this cor- respondence which I forward, as I think it is very hard .that a charge of this kind should be made against a religious community without giving them an oppor- tunity of justifying themselves before the world. lam sure you will earn the gratitude of all my co-religonists by publishing this correspondence. [corv.] Industrial School, Salthill, Ist June, '92.

(To the Editor of the Galway Express.) DHAe Stn,—My attention has been directed to an article in your issue of the 28th ult., under the heading "They would not eat Protestant fish," which entirely misleads the pulelic, and misrepresents our action with regard to the Rev. Mr. Greene's present of three boxes of mackerel to this institution. It is to be regretted that the writer before penning his article did not make himself acquainted with the real facts of the case. There is internal evidence of this, quite independent of the writer's own gratuitous statement, that he received his information from no higher source than "one of our local wits." It is true the fish was presented but not received. The reasons for decline the present as also for delaying reply, are given in the'followieg, letter of the 26th ult. to the Rev. Mr. Greene :

div.head: [coPY st. Joseph's Industrial School,.
div.p: [coPY st. Joseph's Industrial School,.

Balthill, Galway, May '26th, 1892. Ray. Dssa Silt, I wish to offer you some explanation concerning the very awkward circumstances of our returning the three boxes of fish, so kindly presented by you to this Institu- tion on Sunday last. The boys here have quite turned against the use of fish for some time past. We used to supply them with a fish dinner once a week—on Fridays —during the past winter ; however, they did not like it, and at their own request we discontinued it. I wish to remark, that in an Institution of this kind, the manager Is ebliged to be very careful that no cause of discontent may exist. On the occasion when your present came, I feared the inconveniences which might arise even in admitting the article, though it might never be served in the refectory ;more especially as we were just entering on the annual examinations, and any little discontent might cause grave inconveniences. Nevertheless, these circumstances do not lessen your intended kindness, and I beg you will accept our sincere apologies for the unpleasantness of this affair, and our seeming want of appreciation of your well-meant kindness.—With much respect, I am, yours very faithfully, M. R. ROCHE, Manager. Rev. W. J. Greene, Dublin Castle. P.S. This communication would have reached you en Monday morning last, but that the short note accom- panying the present did not contain your address, and • the delay was caused in making inquiries. M. R. R. To the foregoing I received the following reply : MY DEMI SIR, I received yours to-day, and was very glad no mis- take occurred as I had half-concluded. I quite recognise your difficulty, and only regret I did not write to you first—but as I was dealing with a perishable article, I thought I could not get it off to you quick enough. I spent Sunday in Galway docks.—Yours truly, W. J. GREENE.

May 28th, '92. Westport, es. Fingal. In conclusion I will say that anyone who chargec the Irish Catholic Priesthood with intolerance and bigotry, does so without personal knowledge of them. From ex- perience I have in common with thousands of people who have the honour of their acquaintance, and I might say warm-hearted friendship. I can say I always have found them par excellence,impartial and tolerant.' Thank- ing you in anticipation,--I am yours truly, J. C. DALTON.
June 14th, 1892. Warrington,
TIIE GAME OF TORYISM: AN HISTORICAL
RETROSPECT.
Sir,—As a working-man and as one who takes a small
interest in the political affairs of my country, after read- ing and viewing the work and words of the great Con-
servative party, I think as such I may venture a little

criticism. The intellectual destitution of the Conservative party has been made very clear by the extra-parliamentary speeches from among its party. The leaslers, and those who aspire to the leadership from amongst them have nothing to promise which is likely to he of any practical use to the people. Criticism at the best of times is very airy food, and, as the Liberals are always ready to sup ply it for themselves, there is nothing to be gained. by
that of the Conservatives. An attack all alona the line
is being made upon the policy of the Gladstone Govern- ment. The Conservatives are everlastingly telling us
that the Government came into office under unfavourable circumstances. That statement is alrsxost enough to take one's breath away. Why, in 1874 England was at
peace with the whole world, and lir. Gladstone left a surplus of over £5,000,000, for the Tories to commence business with. In 1880 the Liberals returned to power
again, and instead of finding the expenditure of the

country at £74,000,000, as they left it, they found it in- creased to £84,000,000, and instead of a surplus of £5,000,000, they found an increased duty of £9,000,000, and a war legacy of £15,000,000, and, again, they found war and confusion on every side, instead of peace. In 1874 the first speech delivered by the Tory Secretary contained the following passage:—" All I can say is that
at the present moment the position of this country, with regard to our foreign relations, is most satisfactory.
There is no State whatever with which our relations are not the most cordial."

Again,it was convenient for the Conservatives to claim the policy in Egypt as a continuation of their own. That was in the days of success, but when disasters occurred, then the Conservatives discovered that the policy was a blunder and worse than a crime. It is manifestly unjust to charge the Gladstone Government with the Transvaal and Zulu wars. Even political memories cannot be so short as at to recollect that it was the Conservatives who began the war in Zululand, and annexed the Transvaal. All the errors lay in a colonial policy that permitted Sir Bartlett Frere, to indulge in a" forward policy" in Africa, such as he had recommended in the North of India. It was the Conser- vatives that established the dual-control in Egypt, that made France and England liable to the duty of correcting the errors of the Egyptian Government. It was this duality that compelled England to perform a duty in which her partner in the control refused to join her. In all these things whatever errors can be attributed to the Gladstone Government,we have this to remember
that the Conservative Party are responsible for the

initiation of a policy that left very little choice except to fulfil the engagements into which we had entered. I am not going to defend the policy in Africa, but it is due to the Gladstone Government to remember that they did not seek to invade Afghanistan, or Zululand. or to take over the Transvaal, or to administer the finance of Egypt.

_ The Conservatives, had they been in power when the Soudan difficulty came upon us, would have gone in for the conquest of that place, without a thought of the moral consequences, to us as a nation, any more than they would have thought kf the sacrifices of life : for a dream of empire appears to be the one idea of the Con-

servative party. They have not read or have forgotten the history of empires, and the fashion of their rise and fall. Empires decay and disappear, but nations live, and live all the more securely and prosperously as their rulers abstain from ideas of conquest and waste. Egypt,the Transvaal, and Zululand, are only so many elements of weakness to England, and the value of all to us is not sufficient to make up for all the trouble and the loss of life and money in connection therewith. At horne the Gladstone Government had a policy which at least commanded the sym- pathy and received the support of the people at large. One of the greatest measures the Gladstone Government brought forward was the Franchisc; Bill. Mr. Gladstone is and was then a great exponent of self-government. He wished to carry the franchise to the people, and to put the control of the government in the hands of the people who have to pay the taxes, and to take it wholly out of the hands of these who seek in some way or other to get their taxes recouped to them. This, sir, is a great change to the people who appreciate it. But if the House of Commons had passed Lord John Man- ners's amendment it would have been a very serious matter for Parliamentary institutions. The people be- lieved that the House of Commons was representative,but the Tory party laid it down that there being no demand for the franchise it need not be conceded. In plain English, this means that the House of Commons is to be reduced to a &legation to execute the will of the people when violently expressed—say, at Hyde Park or some such place in the United Kingdom. But how was that received by the Tory party ? Why, by the strongest opposition possible. But the Franchise Bill was passed, and along with it a Re-distribution of Seats Rill, both of which have been good and useful measures so far as they went.
Some of the Tories seem ti be very effective speakers • . .

for Tory platforms ; but they weuldnot decrease their efficiency as party orators, if they acquired some ele- mentary knowledge of politics, and some idea of the chronology of events. Some of them are not old enough to remember the Anti-Corn-law struggle that ended in 1846, nor do they know that the Factory legislation which ensued was merely a return match played by the Protec- tionists against the manufacturers who had abolished duties upon corn. All at once the Conservative party was filled with deep concern for the mill hands at the great centres of industry—a concern that they never thought of extending to the agricultural labourers, whose hours were just as long, whose pay was just as bad, and for whom there was just as little sympathy as for the over-worked toilers in manufacturing industries. It is just the same with regard to Sanitary legislation, which they wish to claim for Lord Cross. The Artisans' Dwellings Act, of 1875 was only an attempt to carry into execution plans that Mr. Tort ens had proposed in a more practical form in 1868. Then it pleased the Lords to emasculate Mr. Torrens's Bill ; but in 1875, the very clauses were accepted by the Lords, which seven years ago they had rejected because it was possible to gain some credit for the Conservative party in power. They are equally in error when they come to speak of Tory and Liberal Finance with a certain adroitness that does not represent any candour. They contrast the ex- 1 penditure of the Conservatives and the Liberals—from I 1868 to 1874 for the Liberals, and from 1875 to 1880 for the Tories—by the two first years in each term of office of the two ministers. In 1874 the Liberals left an overflowing exchequer, and for two years the Conservatives kept out ot mis- chief. But what was the case when they went out? There was no surplus; they were in debt; there were liabilities yet to be ascertained. The true basis of comparison is to be found in the two last years of the Tory and the two first of the Liberal government. The expenditure of the latter was more, but why? Because the Liberals were called upon to pay the debts of their predecessors for the wars in Afghanis- tan. in Africa, and in the mysterious course of a policy which was pursued during the Russo-Turkish War. As a matter of fact, the real current expenditure is less, and as another fact it is beyond doubt that in the six years of eory rule we had to pay Thirty-five Millions • more than in the six preced- ing years. But what say the figures in connection with tke Finance of the present Government? This , Salisbury government has in a time of peace expended 118 millions more than their predecessors, the Liberals, though the Liberals had to carry on an expensive war 1 and prepare for threatened hostilities with Russia. The finances of the present Government may be summed up as fellows : They have in time of good trade, increased the amount of taxation from £9,772,759 in 1887, to £98,539,000 in 1892. They have reduced the amount set aside for payment of interest on and repayment of capital on the National Debt, from £28,000,000 to £25,000,000. They have thereby set aside for National , Debt purposes out of the annual expenditure during the ' past six years £156,030,288, as against £171,569,750 for the Gladstone Government ; or, in plain figures, 14 I Imillions less. They have increased the grants in aid of landowners (or in other words it has gone into the „pockets of the landowners) from four to five millions a ' year. They have increased the war expenditure from 32 millions in 1887 to 35 millions in 1892. And they have so muddled the Finance Accounts that it is difficult to getat a true and fair basis of income and expenditure fcr any one year. Now, Sir, I think the Tories should not venture upon such dangerous ground as contrasts in Finance between Tories and Liberals. The Tories seek to get all they can,l and keep all they have got for their own class. The 1 Liberals, at least, spend some money in the direction of the people, yet not perhaps so much as we should like, but it is impossible to get rid of the Tory incubus in the form of perpetual pensions, places, and payments for imaginary services. We know how the Tories hate the Liberals, for there are among them men of true worth and sterling value, and they are a horror to the Tories. A man who would disfranchise a pocket borough, and who would pay an honest salary to a representative is naturally an object of political hate to people who wish to keep family boroughs and enjoy perpetual pensions. The Tories think it consistent to support the titles to land given by'

Igrants from the Crown and the pension list, which was , invented hen there was no more land to give away; but to give a few hundreds a year to representatives duly elt,cted by the people is sacrilege and treason to the constitution! Now, sir, in closing I must say that the Tories hate the Liberals, or Radicals, as they are often called, just as a rat hates a terrier, and their addresses and speeches will have the result of showing us how little they know, and how destitute they and their party are in any present forecast of a policy worthy of the acceptance of the masses of the poople.—Yours, A WORKING-MAN.

div.head: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.
div.p: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.
THE NEW AMALGAMATION.

_ On Tuesday afternoon an extraordinary general meeting of this Banking Company was held at the Bank Premises, Winwick-street, for the purpose of considering, and, if thought fit, passing, a certain resolution relating to the Amalgamation with the Alliance Bank, Limited. Tue new chairman of tho Company, Mr. .2%- Turner, of Elmswood Hall, Aigburth, presided, and other directors present were Colonel Gamble. C. 8., Colonel McCorquodale, Mr. P Stubs, Mr. Cecil Parr, Mr. H. Warren Meade-King: Mr. E. W. Nix, Mr. E. Banbury, Mr. N. F. Eckersley, and Mr. John Dun. There was also a fair attend- ance of shareholders. THE RETIREMENT OF MI LATE CHAIRMAN.-THE REASONS

FOR AMALGAMATION. The CHAIRMA.N read the following letter which he had received from Mr. J. C. Parr, who has recently resigned the chairmanship of the company :—" Dear Mr. Chairman,—l hope my absence from the meeting on the 14th will not be attributed to any lack of inte- rest on my part in the business under discussion. On the contrary, it is my earnest wish that the new depar- ture you meet to inaugurate may prove a signal success, and that the amalgamated bank may maintain that high reputation achieved by Parr's Banking Company ; but I feel that a formal leave-taking, after resigning a chairmanship which I have held for eighteen years, is a trial I shall be gladly spared. I hope at some future time, however, to say a few words in grateful thanks for the uniform suppof t and sympathy I have invari- ably met with at the hands of the shareholders during the long series of years I have had the honour of presi- ding over your meetings.—Yours truly, J. CHARLTON Pam" Ha (the Chairman) said he could not occupy that seat without personally emphasizing the expres- sions of regret and sorrow which they had read in the circulars issued to them—regret that their late chairman, Mr. Parr, who so well, and so successfully, for 18 years fulfilled the duties which he had been called upon to un- dertake, should have retired from the chairmanship, and sorrow for the death of their late Deputy-Chairman, Mr. Eckersley, and of Mr. Edward Greenall (chairman of the Select Committee), men whose ripe experience, sound judgment, and acknowledged position were most valu- able, and whose devotion and zeal were most beneficial to the Bank. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Referring to the amalgamation, he said they had not been long in London before they foend that the premises in Lombard- street, though admirably situated, were far too small for their business. They not only precluded the possi- bility of any extension, but absolutely choked the cur- rent stream I Their customers were inconvenienced and urgent in their remonstrances. They tried but failed to acquire the adjoining premises. They looked, but with- out success, for suitable ones elsewhere. They found they should have to build. This would have incurred an outlay of sometking like £150,000, involving a serious loss of interest during building. The only alternative was amalgamation with some bank possessing the accommodation they required. This, fortunately, they had met with. It was not always that amalgamations were equally advantageous to the contracting parties, that one did not think that he had given too much, or the other that he had received too little. In the present instance, the shareholders of both banks received sub- stantial benefit, and lsy their union formed an establish- ment which, with its paid up capital of a million, and a reserve fund of a similar amount, might fairly be en- titled to take a position amongst the leading backs of the United Kingdom. In the amalgamation, the Directors were simply following a course which had led the Company to its present prosperous condition; and he held in his hand an official report of its career, which showed that their bank, had absorbed, by putchase or amalgamation, banking businesses in the following places, viz. :—Northwich, from Messrs. Thos. Firth and Son in 1865 ; Macclesfield, from the Metropolitan and Provincial Bank in 1867 ; Wigan, from Messrs. Woodcock, Sons, and Eckersley, in 1874; Leek, from Mr. F. W.Jennins,rs, in 1877 ; Chester, from Messrs. Dixons and Co., in 1878; Liverpool, with Birkenhead, Bootle, and Waterloo, from the National Bank of Liverpool, Limited, in 1883 ; London, 77, Lom- bard-st.' from Messrs. Fuller, Banbury, Nix and Co., in 1891." He should like, before sitting down, to mention with very great pleasure, that the Board had that day elected Mr. Cecil F. Farr to the office of deputy-chair- man. He congratulated him, as he congratulated him- self, on having such an able vice-chairman bearing the venerated name of Parr. (Applause.)

, VOTE OF THANKS TO THE LATE CHAIRMAN. Mr. ROM.RT DAVIES moved, "That the shareholders pass an expression of regret at the retirement of Mr. Parr from the chairmanship, and thank him for the valuable services he has rendered as head of the Bank during the past 18 years." He said he felt that there was not a single shareholder, absent or present, who would not cordially concur in the vote of thanks. They were all very grateful indeed to him for the a*lility and care he had exercised, and they regretted very much to lose him. At the same time, after 18 years' services, they felt that he was quite justified in retiring,especially as the Rank seemed to be entering upon a new phase of its existence. Witik regard to their present chair- man, he had been connected with him in a matter of business, and it was impossible for any man to behave in a more honourable manner than he did throughout that business. He, therefore, in the name of the shareholders, he welcomed Mr. Turner as their Chairman and he felt very satisfied indeed that Mr. Cecil F. • Parr had undertaken the office held by their lamented friend, Mr. Eckersley. He had looked into the amalgamation with tne greatest care and_ aS far as his judgement went, he cordially agreed

with it. Mr. ROBERT PIBRPOINT seconded the motion, and said he wished to emphasize the feeling of regret at losing the services of Mr. Parr as chairman of the bank, but they were pleased to know that he would remain one of the directors, and that his brother would be the Deputy- Chairman of the Bank. The resolution was then put and carried unanimously. TELE DRAFT AGRY.Mikair.

The CiEnumtnx moved "That the draft agreement submitted to this meeting, and expressed to be made between the Alliance Bank Limited and its liquidators of the one part. and Parr's Banking Company Limited of the other part, be and the same is hereby approved, and that the Directors be and they are hereby authorized to enter into an agreement in terms of the said draft, and to carry the same into effect with such (if any) modification as they think expedient." This was seconded by rk Ir. Cecil F. Parr, and carried.

div.head: TEM NAME AND 'CAPITAL OF THE COMPANY.
div.p: TEM NAME AND 'CAPITAL OF THE COMPANY.

It was decided that the name of the company be changed to " Parr's Banking Company and the Alliance Bank, Limited." The CHAIRMAN said it was rather a long name, but it had been thought desirable to keep well in the foreground that it was Parr's Banking Com- pany, and not merely " Parr's and Alliance Bank." There were lonzer names than their own. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) It was decided, en the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. CECIL F. PARR, "That the capital of the Company shall be increased to £5,000,000 by the creation of 17,506 shares of £lOO each." Other resolutions incidental to the Amalgamation were also adopted. ELECTION OF A DIRECTOR. On the motion of Captain WITHINGTON, seconded byf Mr. J. R. BUC&TON, it was resolved "That the election o' Mr. N. Farington Eckersley as a director be' confirmed.' A vote of thanks to the Chairman, moved by Dr. Starkey Smith, and seconded by Mr. T. B. Dakin, con- cluded the business.

MEETING OF THE ALLIANCE BANK. A special 'meeting of the shareholders in the Alliance Bank was held on Tuesday,at the Cannon-st. Hotel, Lon- ' don,for the purpose of authorising an amalgamation with Parr's Banking Company.—Sir L. Playfair presided, and explained the conditions upon which the directors of the two banks had come to a provisional arrangement after prolonged negotiations. He thought they had arrived at an amalgamation which'would be advantageous to both banks. Parr's Banking Company was one of the oldest- established of the provincial banks; it had large connec- tions, having forty-three branches in Lancashire and Cheshire ; and it had a large earning power, its usual dividend being 19 per cent. It was, however, chiefly a provincial hank. Its London connections were nothing like those of the Alliance Bank, which had twelve metropolitan branches ; but the earning power of the latter was not nearly so great, being only 8 per cent. The amalgamation gave each bank what was lacking in the other. It gave Parr's Bank a large influential London connection, 4nd it gave the Alliance Bank a considerable provincial connection. The amalgamated banks would have a capital of £5.000,000, of which £1,000,000 was paid, and there would be a reserve fund of £1,000,000. The deposit and current accounts amounted to £12,000,000 in the two banks, against which there would be securities amount- ing to £17,835,384. He moved a resolution authorizing amalgamation, which was seconded by Mr. Dun, and agreed to unanimously after some discussion.

The labour correspondent of the Board of Trade, in his periodical memorandum, states that there is an in- crease in the number of strikes recorded, but this, how ever, is owing to improved prospects in the various trades.

TG THE ELECTORS OF THE WIDNES DIVIdION CF SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE. GENTLFIYIEI, —At the nuanlmous request of the District Liberal Councils, I h.ve consented to stand as the Li berm Candidate for the Widnes Division at the General Election ; the time has now come to ask for your votes and interest- As I have always lived in Widnes. I am well-known to most of you, and since my Bele: tion by the District Councils I have had many opportunities of explaining to you my views on the political questions of the day. If electedas your representative in Parliament, I shall give a hearty support to Mr. Gladstone's Irish Policy, for I be- lieve that in granting Home Rule to Ireland we shall perform au act of justice which will bring peace and happiness to that country. I feel confident that Home Rule can be granted to ths Irish nation not only without the slightest danger of " separation" or " disruption of the Empire," but to the great advantage of the United Kingdom. I am in favour of the Disestsblielsment and Disendow- ment of the Church in Wales, because they are desired by the Welsh people, and because I believe, it to be an intolerable injustice to maintain the Marsh of the minority as an Established Church against the will•of Ihe large majority. It is my earnest intention to assist so far as I can in ameliorating the conditions of labour, and in removing legis- lative obstacles which hinder the working classes in their efforts to improve their lot. 'With these objects in view lam In favour of an extension of the Factory Acts, of the insertion in all contracts issued by the Government or public bodies of provisions against " sweating " of the amendment of the Employers' Liability Act, and of a reform of the Poor Laws. The hours of labour when they are excessive should be shortened. I shall, if elected, support the Miners' Eight Hours Bill, and I will give most careful consideration to legia. Lstive proposals of a similar nature. The welfare of the community requires a reform of the Licensing Laws. lane in hearty agreement with the prin- ciple of the Direct Veto, and am in favour of Sunday Closing and the transference of the licensing powers to a popularly elected representative body, Th e interest which I have always taken in Educational matters is well known to you. I look for an extension of our system of National Education, so that the children of the poor, no less than those of the rich, may receive the highest possible training wherever they show the neeeaa:rs capacity for it. The system Rf Techni •al Instruction, in my opinion. also requires to be greatly improved and developed. I approve of a thorough reform ef the Land Laws, to obtain amongst other things, the repeal of the laws Of primogeniture and entail, the freedom of sale and transfer, and the en- franchisement of leaseholders. The condition of the rural population demands immediate attention, and lam in favour ef the creation of District and Parish Councils endowed with compulsory powers of acquir- ing land for allotments and public purposes at fair prices, and entrusted with the management of local affairs. If elected, I shall support proposals for the reform of the Registration Laws and the adoption of the principle of "One Man One Vote"; the Payment of Members of Parliament and the cffi.eial expenses of Rettuning, Officers. lam also in favour of shorter Parliaments and the "mending or ending" of the House of Lords. Changes in the Incidence of Taxation are imperatively needed to secure the taxation of ground :values and mining royalties, the equaliz Aim of the death duties, the division.of rates between owner and sccupier, and a "free breakfast table." If you do me the honour 6f returning me as your represen- tative to the House of Commons I shall endeavour to the best of my ability, to promote the welfare of our cettatty, and to further and protect the interests of the electors of the Whines Divis'on.—l am, Gentlemen, your Obeilent Ser- vant, Appleton House, Widnes, June. 1892.
H. WADE DEACON.
THE REPRESENTATION OF WIDNES.

MR. WADE DEACON'S CAMPAIGN. The Campaign in Widnes is now in full swing. and it will be seen from the reports given below that several meeting& have been held during the week. Last night there was a crowded gathering, in the Widnes Drill Hall in support of Mr. H. Wade Deacon, the Liberal candidate, and the pro- ceedings were Gf he r•ost enthusiastic kind. We hold over a reuoi. ch the meeting until our next issue. Mr. Deacon has issued an admirable address which appears in this column, and which we com- mend to the attention of the electors. It is satisfactory to say that he ha 3 every prospect of winning the seat.
the supporters the al

On Monday evening a meeting of ,of Mr. 11. Wade Deacon the Liberal candidate for ! Widnes Division, was held in the Welsh Chapel, !Layton Quarry. There was a good attendance and Mr. J. B. Leach presided. . Mr. Deacon before delivering his address, moved the following resolution :—" That this meeting of Huyton Liberals hails wiih satisfaction the approaching dissolu- tion as affording an opportunity of expressing through ! the ballot box their conscientious support of Mr. Glad- stone's Irish policy, and of reversing the hastily con- ceived and mistaken verdicts given by the constituency at the two last general elestions.' Mr. Deacon said the day for the election was approaching, and if they were united he believed they had every chance of winning. (Applause.) Unity was what they wanted ; and in Tot- ing they sheuld remember they were voting for the Liberal cause. Ile had not a word to say against Mr. GRIM personally ; but politically it was a different mat- ter. He had read Mr. Gilliat's speech, but he could not make out what policy he really advocated. There was one remark made by his opponent with which he agreed—that the Irish question must be kept to the ! front. (Applause.) Well, if that gentleman had been longer in the district he would havo known that the Irish question had always been to the front in that division. ! As to the remark that there had been no more coercion in Ireland than in England, he would point out that the C( erci,m Act was never directed against ordinary crime or to the strengthening of the ordinary law. Crime in Ireland had always been smaller in proportion than in England; but dating the last few years there had been a slight increase, so that whatever the Coercion Act had done it had not touched the ordinary crime in that coun- try. Coercion had been used arbitrarily to suppress public meetings and interfere with the liberty of the Press. New, why had the Tories lately backed out of coercion? The truth was the general elec- tion was approaching; and, as had often been the case, when the elctions came round coercion retired. (Applause.) Mr. Deacon also dealt with the i mportance of land reform and a reduction in min- ing royalties. In that manufacturing district cheap coal, so long as the miner received a fair wage and the proprietor a fair return, was absolutely necessary. He gave instances of how excessive royalties had ruined some mining industries. In this country the royalty on each ton of coal averaged 53. as against ed. in Ger- many, Bd. in France, and Is. 31. in Belgium. A reform in such a matter was urgently needed. In conclusion, Mr. Deacon said they had a great and inspiriting cause to fight for—(hear, hear)—the cause of freedom and justice as against injustice and privilege. (Applause.) Mr. W. Gerrard seconded the resolution which was sup- ported by Mr. Ellis J. Griffiths (Liberal candidate of West Toxteth) and carried unanimously. THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE AT woouroN. A public meeting of the Liberals residing in the Wool- ton district of the Widnes Division was held on Tuesday ! evening in the schoolroom, Wootton, to hear an address from Mr. Wade-Deacon, the Liberal candidate. Mr T. E. Timmin occupied the chair. The meeting room was crowded, among those preset being Messrs. J. IL Carey, S. K. Mospratt, R. Craig, G. Timmis, Gossage, E. Jones, Stewart Deacon, and H. B. Shores.—The Chairman regretted the cause of the retirement of Mr. Edwards-Moss from public life, and said that they all hoped that his health might soon be restored. They did not, however, want him again as the representative of the Widnes Division.—Mr. Deacon said " That the, Government reminded hiin of a timid person with a bad tooth who feared to go to the dentist, in that they were afraid to go before the electors. In that district they had every reason to be hopeful of the result of the election when it did come if they would sink petty differ- ences and pull together—not necessarily for the candi- date as a candidate, but for the Liberal party at large. He then dealt with Mr. Gilliat's speeches, and said he could hardly see what Mr. Gilliat's programme was, if, indeed, lie had one. With regard to the land question, he would advocate cheap transfer of land, and said that if they desired any legislation on this question they must look to the Liberal party for it, as it was not likely that the Conservative party would do much in that way to benefit the people. He did not, however, believe that Ulster would rebel. If Home Rule was I passed, as it would be shortly, they would receive it with quietude, as good citizens should. (Applause.)— Mr. Eustace Carey seconded the resolution, which was supported by Mr. J. Herbert Lewis, and carried. CONSERVATIVE MEETINGS. Mr. J. S. Gilliat, M.P., the Conservative candidate for the Widnes Division, attended on Monday evening at the Conservative Club, Widnes, for the purpose of meeting the members of the club and the district polling commit- tee. The proceedings were of an informal character. Mr. R. Lewis, chairman of the north polling district, pre- sided, and among those present were Messrs. J. White, W. T. Husband, T. A. Bullough, W. Tracey, sen., J. W. White, S. Patin, J. Knowles, W. R. Madge, secretary of the Ih'idracs Division, and ethers. Mr. Gilliat briefly addressed the assembly upon vari- ous topics, chiefly with regard to his candidature. The season he did not seek re-election for Clapham Division

was because he feared some time ago his health would not permit him to encounter another political conflict, I and because a successor had been found in whom he could trust the future of the constituency. Referring to political matters he said Ireland had had six years of resolute Government, and Ireland did not block the way from a Conservative point of view. Thecondition of the sister isle was better than it was six years ago, and it would be still better if the present government was returned to power. (Applause.) Touching upon the labour question, he said he believed he understood the needs of the labouring classes, and he viewed with resentment the severing of the bonds between the classes and the masses.

On Tuesday night a well-attended meeting of Con- servatives and Liberal-Unionists was held in the Drill Hall, Widnes, in support ef the candidature of Mr. Gilliat. M.P., for the Clapham Division. Major Cross, chairma. Id the Widnes Division, Conservative, presided. Mr. Gilliat, who was well received, remarked that he had no mean opponent before him. Mr. Wade Deacon was a man who in Widnes deserved every respect and regard in his personal character, and if it were not that he was an exponent of principles from which he utterly dissented, it would be extreme audacity for him (Mr. Gilliat) in Widnes to oppose a local man of such high character. He said coercion, which the Conservative Government had carried, had been successful up to the present time. In consequence of those six years of reso- lute government agrarian crime had been reduced from 632 cases annually to practically nil at the present time. Ile (Mr. Gilliat) had been challenged as being unlit to represent a commercial community, but if he had no other claims, it was sufficient that he had been interested in the commerce and finance of this country for 40 years. (Applause.) Mr. R. Lewis then moved a resolution pledging the meeting to use every legitimate means to ensure Mr. Gill i at's election. Mr. J. White seconded the resolution, which was carried, and the meeting ended.

div.head: WIDNES TRADES COUNCIL AND THE ELECTION. QUESTIONS TO CANDIDATES.
div.p: WIDNES TRADES COUNCIL AND THE ELECTION. QUESTIONS TO CANDIDATES.

Recently the Trades Council of Widnes and dis- trict. forwarded to the parlimentary candidates for the Widnes and Northwich Parliamentary Divisions, the following list of questions :-1. Are you in fav- our of legislation regulating hours of labour to eight hours per day in all trades and oc- cupations, save where a majority of the organised members of any trade or occupation protest by a ballot voting against the same ? 2. Extension of the Factory Acts to laund- ries, domestic workshops, bake-houses and all other trades and occupations where women, and children are employed, and raising the age of half-timers to twelve years. (3) The appoint- ment of sufficient sub-inspectors for factories,workshops mines, railways, add merchant shipping. (4) Payment of members of Parliament and returning officers' official expenses by the State. (5) The issue of certificates of competency to all men having charge of engines and boilers by the Board of Trade ; six months' charge prier to the passing of the Act to be deemed sufficient evi- dence of capacity. (6) Abolition of property qualifica- tion for representive public offices. (7) Employers' Liability Act being amended by abolishing the doctrine of common employment, leaving the amount of com- pensation to the discretion of a jury, and rendering illegal all contracting out of the Act •, extending the Act to seamen ; also extending notice of intention to pro- ceed under the Act for six weeks to six months. (8) Preventing importation of pauper foreign labour. (9) Amending the laws of conspiracy so that no act done in'combination, unless criminal in itself, shall be illegal. (10) Inserting the" sweating" clause in Government contracts. Mr. H. W. Deacon, Liberal candidate for Widnes Division, replies that he is in favour of the legislative regulation of hours of labour in certain cases, but does not think it wise to apply restrictive legislation to all trades at once, especially in view of the different opin- ions held amongst working men themselves. He replies " Yes " te questions 2,3, and 4, and in regard to query 5 says that he is strongly inclined to agree with the pro- posal. Question 6, yes. 7. Ido not see why the bene- fit of the Act should not be extended to seamen, but I do not know enough of the merits of the case to pledge myself ;to the next question I reply, yes. R. I shall, if elected, consider any proposal on this subject. We have hitherto prided ourselves upon the fact that our country was free to the oppressed, and I think that few of us would wish to refuse to shelter any people suffering under religious persecution; at the same time, as other countries have recently taken action to pre- vent the landing on their shores of paupers from foreign countries, we may be compelled to take action in self- defence. 9. Yes. 10. Ido not exactly know what the sweating clause' is to which you refer ; but I am in favour of Government doing its very utmost to prevent sweating." Mr. Brunner, M.P. for the Northwich Division, says with regard to the payment of members of Parliament and of returning officers' charges by the State, and to the abolition of property qualification for representa- tive public offices, he replies in the affirmative, adding that these are genuine, far-reaching reforms making for freedom and equality. He should encourage every measure designed to make it as easy as possible for every citizen, rich or poor, who had earned the respect of his fellows, to serve either upon local authorities or in Parliament. It was one of the scandals of the pre- sent Parliament that no serious and earnest attempt had been made to pass an Employers' Liability Act on the lines indicated in the question, and that Mr. Robertson's Bill in 1891, and his re- solution in 1892, to amend the laws of con- spiracy, were voted down by a majority of Minis- terialists and Liberal -Unionists. He was prepared (question 2) to extend the operation of the Faistories Acts to laundries, domestic workshops, and to trades and occupations where young children and women are employed, wherever, after full inquiry, such an exten- sion was proved necessary and desirable. He should continue to vote for the raising of the age of half-timers to twelve years. With regard to question 5, he was not convinced that men could not be entrusted to take charge of engines or boilers without a certificate of com- petency from the Board of Trade. He was orepared to give full consideration to the forthcoming Government measure regarding the importation of foreign labour, laut it seetned to him clear that the policy of shutting the doors against labourers from other lands would ulti- mately result in making Englishmen suffer more than any one else. He approved of the insertion of clauses in contracts securing for workmen the hours of labour and the rate of wages sanctioned by the organised trades unions, and was strongly in favour of reducing the hours of labour of workmen. A limit of hours should accomplished by combination. He could not see his way to support a Bill enacting a universal eight hours day for all trades and occupations. Mr. G. Wniteley, Conservative candidate for the Northwich Division, states that he is not in favour of an eight Hours Bill for all trades, but would support one for miners, and would also favour the limitation of working hours for responsible railway employes. In answer to question two, he was favourable to both mat- ters, but should like the opinions of the trades con- cerned as to them. In the trade in which he was engaged (cotton) the operatives objected to the raising of the age of half-timers, and if that feieling was general he should respect it. Questions 3,5, 8,7, and 9 he answers in the affirmative. but (question 4) does not favour payment of all members. Favouring the increase of direct labour representation, he would support a reasonable annual allowance to accredited representa- tivos of trade organisations. He would favour any action to put a stop to the abominable practice of sweat-
ing. Mr. J. S. Gilliat, Conservative candidate for Widnes, has not forwarded a written reply to the questions, but is referring to them in his election speeches.

div.head: WA.RIIINGTON AND THE DISSOLUTION.
div.p: WA.RIIINGTON AND THE DISSOLUTION.

The announcement made by Mr. Balfour with re- gard to the coming dissolution of Parliament has stimulated political activity in Warrington as in other parts of the country. Both parties have been actively canvassing for some weeks, and the work is now being pursued with renewed energy. Mrs. llouston reached Warrington on Wednesday, and will, we understand, be joined by 'llr. Houston to- day. Pr. Houston will remain in Warrington and be actively engaged in the campaign until the election is over. The canvass on behalf of the Liberal party is in a fairly forward state, and is so satisfactory in its results that there is every hope of the Liberal candidate being returned. It is desirable that all Liberals who can help in the canvass and in other ways should immediately put themselves in com- munication with the officials of the party at the Liberal Club.

div.head: PROBABLE DAY OF ELECTION.
div.p: PROBABLE DAY OF ELECTION.

- -- In the event of the dissolution taking place, as it is expected to do, on Tuesday, the 28th lust, the Mayor will, we understand, in all probability, tlx the Tuesday followmg, July sth, as the day of the election. The nominations would take place on Saturday, the 2nd July, and the election would of necessity have to be held on one of the three days following, excluding Sunday.

THE RECENT RAILWAY ACCIDENTS. Yesterday, the adjourned inquest on Joseph Allen, of Halifax, one of the victims of the:Esholt railway accident, concluded at Guiseley. and resulted in a verdict of " Accidental death," McClay, the driver, being acquitted of the charge of culpable negligence.—The inquest on the five persons who died at Leeds stands adjourned until Friday next.

div.head: MURDER BY ITALIANS. FOUR MEN LYNCHED.
div.p: MURDER BY ITALIANS. FOUR MEN LYNCHED.

SBATLE, WASHINGTON,FRIDAY.—John Nelson, foreman of a gang of Italian labourers on the Monte Christ° Railway, Ledro, Washington, was attacked yesterday, by four Italians, and killed, being struck down with an iaon bar. The friends hf Nelson, to the number of 60, seized the Italians, and in the presence of 150 of their countrymen, lynched them. THE ULSTER CONVENTION.—GREAT GATHERING AT BELFAST. A telegram from Belfast, dated 10-30 a-m, says : The doors were opened at a quarter-past eleven, and the vast convention buildings, estimated to hold about 12,000 people were steadily filled. Precisely at noon, the Duke of Abercorn entered, and amid cheers was chosen as president og the convention. The Duke of Abercorn delivered the presidential address. He des- ' cribed the meeting as a great demonstration, vast in its extent and solemn in its nature. In conclusion, his Grace said, "We will not have Home Rule," words which were received with prolonged cheering by the whole audience upstanding. Sir William Ewart then moved the first resolution, ex- pressing the loyalty of the Ulster Unionists t the Crowrt, avowing their resolve to retain unchanged their present position, and determination to have nothing to do with a Parliament certain to be controlled by men responsible for crime and outrage. Mr. Thomas Sinclair Presbyterian, and a Liberal Unionist, in seconding the resolution, denied that the people of Ulster made any demand for Protestant ascendancy. The resolution was adopted. A vote of thanks to the Duke of Abercorn for presiding, having been adopted the proceedings con- cluded at three o'clock, with the singing of the National Anthem and benediction. A monster demonstration was afterwards held in the Botanic Gardens, close to the Convention building, the Lord Mayor of Belfast presiding at the principal of the three platforms from which the addresses were de- livered. About 70,000 people were said to have been present,

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at four o'clock., The Duke of York, introduced by the Prince of Wales and the Duke of Connaught, took his seat with the cus- tomary ceremonies on his elevation. The Mersey and Irwell (Prevention of Pollution) Bill passed a second reading. The House went into Committee on the Small Agricul- tural Holdings Bill. The House adjourned at quarter-past eight. HOUSE OF COMMONS. - •
The Speaker took the chair shortly after three o'clock. The Standing orders were suspended, and the Lanca- shire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Railway Bill was read a third time.

..... RECENT RAILWAY COLLISIONS.-Sir M. HICES-BEACH answering Mr. Dixon, said the signal in default in the cases of the recent serious collisions at Birmingham and Leeds was not a signal sanctioned by the Board of Trade, but a signal used under special circumstances.

div.head: DISSOLUTION.
div.p: THE DISSOLUTION.

Mr. GLADSTONE, who was received with Oppositicn cheers, asked the First Lord of the Treasury if he could now state what were the measures to be proceeded with, and tke particular day for the dissolution of Parliament. Mr. BALFOUR said the request was a reasonable one. The session cibuld not be brought to a close before the business of the other House had been cc 'eluded, and they had sent and were In the act of sending up a largo number of bills to them, and there was no possibility of those bills being dealt with before the end of the week. He proposed to adjourn the House on Wednesday, but the following Monday would have to be kept open in case of the Lords' amendments. The dissolution, there- fore, could not possibly take place before Wednesday or Thursday, the 29th or 30th—(" Oh, oh ")—and not before Monday the 27th. ATTACK ON THE GOVERNMENT.

Mr. LABOUCHERB then asked leave to move the ad- journment of the House in order te call attention to the delay of the date of the dissolution, owing to the action of the House of Lords not being prepared to deal with the Bills placed before it. Leave was given, the whole of the Opposition, includ- ing the front bench, standing up in favour of it. Mr. LAnotrenEns very briefly stated that the House of Lords was the stumbling block in the way, and that but for that branch of the Legislature the business could be disposed of by Wednesday next. Sir W. Heaconwr, who was received with Opposition cheers, said the acts of the Government would do them no good, and would be met with resentment by a major- ity of the electors who would lose them many votes. (Opposition cheers.) Mr. BILFOUR rising amidst loud Ministerial cheers, said so far as his own observations went Saturday was the most disfranchising of all days. Since the hours of polling had been extended to eight o'clock no,disfran- chisment of a large kind could operate with regard to the working classes, whereas an enormous multitude of smaller tradesmen would be unable to vote on a Satur- day. Mr. GIADSTONIE said it appeared to his observation and memory the first time the House of Lords had given such careful attention to bills that went to them from this House. Professor Stuart and Mr. Goscheh follov7ed.
On Mr. Balfour's motion it was agreed that at the con- clusion of public business to-day, the House adjourned till Monday. The remaining orders having been disposed of, the House adjourned at 5-45.

div.head: TRIENNIAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: TRIENNIAL ELECTIONS.

The Clerk submitted C07.17e5-p-o-n-den-C-e-- With Warrington and Falmouth with respect to the cost of the poll, taken to decide whether the ratepayers approved of triennial elections of Guardians, and the Clerk said on the basis of contested elections the cost of taking the poll in Run- corn Union would be about £l5O to £l6o.—Mr. Heywood moved that the Local Government Board be asked to send an order authorising a poll of the ratepayers. He drew attention to the great advantage of triennial elec- tions on the present system, and with regard to the financial aspect said there was a certain saving to the Union of £l3 6s. Bd. a year, so that he considered the £l6O it would cost to take the poll as a good investment. At Runcorn, where there were frequently elections, an election cost £35, and this would be saved two years out of three. There would also be a great saving to Frod- sham, Appleton, and other places, where there were con- tests.—The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. Aaron, Mr. Brandreth, and ethers.—Mr. P. Hall and Mr. W. Whitlow opposed.—The motion was carried by 14 votes to nil. It was decided to hold the poll in October.

VOTE BY BALLOT. Mr. Williams then moved that a petition be sent to the Local Government Board requesting them to take the necessary steps to alter the mode of election of Guardians to that of vote by ballot. Upwards of 100 Boards of Guardians, he said,had petitioned in this way. —Mr. Lea seconded ,tlie motion, which was carried un- animously.
THE CHILDREN'S TRIP. Mr. Cunnah, the master, announced that the response to his appeal for subscriptions on behalf of the children's trip to Blackpool in July had been most generous.

July Ist. 1892, until further notice. The traffic will be received and forwarded via the Weston Paint Docks, or via the Ship Canal through Eastham Locks. COUNTY OF CHESTER, TO WIT. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER, will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 27th day of June instant, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hun- dreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all pri- seners committed from such Hundreds will take place at such 'Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 27th day of June instant, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE COURT will be Adjourned ty the Court House, Nether Knutsford, on WRDNiSDAY, the 29th day of June instant, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be ernpannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arrising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Ad- journed Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on Wan- NISDAT. the 29th day of June instant, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester, 7th June, 1892.

Parkinson, Mather, and Co. SECERTARY.—WiIIiaM Bralsford. OFFICES.-73, Icing-street, Manchester. THE TRUST FUND SYSTEM. The Directors of the Manchester Trust Limited, recognis- ing the need of other facilities than those already afforded for the investment of money by way of deposit, have decided to give special attention to this class of t usiness. and have taken suitable premises at No. 73, Ring-at., Manchester, for the purpose. They have accordingly arranged the system of secdrity set forth as follows. One of the principal features of the system they have devised is the establishment by trust deed of Specific Trust Funds, whereby, independently of the credit and resources of the Manchester Trust it-elf, with its subscribed capital of £500,000 and reserves, securities at least equal to the amount of the deposits must always be held absolutely charged as security to the depositors. The security thus obtained is of an absolute character, and ,constitutesfor the depositor an insured and guaranteed in- vestment. both as to capital and income, free from all market .fluctuations and vicissitudes. The depositors in each fund will be secured (Firstly).—,By a first charge upon the securities lodged in tke fund. (Secondly). —By the guarantee of the Manchester Trust Limited. The Manchester Trust Limited will receive on deposit large or small sums (not under £10). For sums of £53 or over the Trust will issue certificates in the registered name of the depositor. These will be transfer- able by special transfer form and can he sold and transferred I at any time, like consols, bonds, or shares. Deposits may be for fixed terms, at fixed rates of interest, or the Trust will issue certificates, with coupons for the Interest attached payable half-yearly, which may be arranged for special dates. These notes will be re-payable any half- year on seven days' notice. Large sums of over £l,OOO may if desired, be treated as a special trust fund, to which specific securities may be allocated. For sums under £5O (or over that amount if desired for the convenience of the depositors) pass books will be issued, re- payment being made either at fixed dates or on seven days' notice. The .various trust deeds have been settled byconnsel,Frank L. Weight, Bag., and can be seen at the offices of the Man- chester Trust, Limited, 73, King-st., Manchester. GENERAL SECURITIES FUND. A.—Certificates for sums of £5O or over will be issued, and interest allowed in tins fund asunder, viz. : For six months 4 per cent per annum. For ,twelve months For two years 4- per cent per annum. For three years 4f per cent per annum. For deposits withdrawalable at the end of any six months on seven days' notiee 4 per cent, per annum. B.—Pass Books: For sums under £5O (or over that amount desired•for the convenience of the depositor) pass books will be issued, repayment being made either at fixed dates or on seven days' notice. The rates of interest for fixed terms will be the same as above. For money withdrawable at any time on seven days' notice interest at the rate of 3i per cent per annum will be allowed. THE MORTGAGE SECURITIES FUND. This fund wilLcomprise mortgage securities only, For deposits fixed or one year and under three years the interest allowed will be 31 per cent. per annum, but if for three years and upwards the rate will be 4 per cent, per annum, -- DEPOSITS ON OPEN ACCOUNT. Moneys (250 or over) will also be received on deposit out- side these trust funds on promissory not., as under : For shr months 4- per cent per annum. For twelve months 4i. per cent per annum. For three years andupwards 41 per cent per annum. Full information in respect of any of the before-mentioned funds may be had on application to the secretary of THE MANCHESTER TRUST LIMITED, WM. BRELSFORD. Secretary. 73, King-street, Manchester,

THE SHIP CANAL. _- SEIZURE OF DRINK ON THE CANAL WORKS AT NORTON. The. Runcorn police have for some time been sus- picious that the illicit sale of drink has been conducted on an extensive sale on the works of the Manchester Ship Canal, at the Big Field, Norton. On Wednesday, Supt. Atherton, accompanied by Inspector Coeper and several officers made a raid on one of tne huts, in which they discovered casks of beer and bottles of spirits. These- they immediately seized, and had conveyed to the Police Station at Runcorn. Summonses are being issued against the offenders. It is believed that the illicit sale of drink is largely practised, and the police antici- pate making still further discoveries. FATALITY AT RUNCORN. Yesterday at noon, Samuel Hitchen, aged 16 years pr age, 21, Norfolk-st., was killed oia the Ship Canal rail- way, at Old Quay, Runcorn. The deceased was em- ployed as a wagon gr easer, and when he was coming between two sets of wagons, they were set in motion by a wagon bumping against ten, and he wag crushed between the buffers. His back Was broken and death was instanteous. PENKETH. -- THR PARK COMPANY. The Penketh Park Company are rapidly peehhig forward with their work. A brickyard has been started near the baths, and the foundations for several cottages have been laid. The baths stilt remain in an unfinished state. PIGEON SHOOTING.
